projectTitle: Brindlewood Industrial: The API That Trusted the Wrong Thing
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish ServiceNow scoped application build for a fictional industrial manufacturer -- a real partner self-service application taken from data model through a row-level ACL, a Service Portal, Flow Designer automation, and a Scripted REST API, then a genuine cross-partner data leak caught by a pre-launch security review, not by a partner finding it first.
businessContext: Brindlewood Industrial is an industrial equipment manufacturer with about 1,800 employees and a network of roughly 200 authorized third-party service partners. Partners submit warranty claims by phone and email into a shared inbox -- claims get lost, status is invisible, and partners' own field-service software has no way to check in programmatically. Natalie Fairweather (Director of Partner Operations) wants partners to self-serve, safely -- Brindlewood's partners often compete directly against each other in the same local markets, so a cross-partner data leak would be a serious trust failure, not just a technical bug. Dmitri Kowalski (ServiceNow Developer) builds the scoped application, its ACL, portal, automation, and API; Zara Ahmed (ServiceNow Technical Architect) runs the pre-launch security review that finds a real vulnerability in the API nobody caught in UAT.
architectureSummary: A scoped application (x_brind_claims, "Partner Warranty Claims") with a custom Warranty Claim table, a row-level ACL restricting each partner to their own company's records, a partner-facing Service Portal, Flow Designer automation routing new claims to the right reviewer, and a Scripted REST API so partners' own field-service software can create and query claims programmatically. ATF test coverage and a pre-launch UAT with real partner accounts both passed cleanly. The real defect wasn't in the ACL, which was correct from the start -- it was in the Scripted REST API's GET handler, which filtered strictly by whatever partner_company value a caller supplied using plain GlideRecord, which does not enforce ACLs the way the native UI does, and never checked that value against who was actually authenticated.

lessons.title: Meeting Brindlewood Industrial: 200 Partners, One Inbox
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Brindlewood Industrial's 200 third-party service partners submit warranty claims by phone and email into a shared inbox -- claims get lost, partners can't see status, and their own field-service software has no way to check in. What Dmitri Kowalski has to learn before any configuration happens.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish ServiceNow scoped-application build for a real business problem at a fictional industrial equipment manufacturer, **Brindlewood Industrial**. Brindlewood makes heavy equipment and keeps about 1,800 employees on staff, but it doesn't service most of that equipment itself -- a network of roughly **200 authorized third-party service partners** handles repairs and field service across the territories Brindlewood can't cover directly.

Here's the actual problem: when one of those partners repairs a piece of Brindlewood equipment under warranty, they have to tell Brindlewood about it to get paid for the labor and parts. Today that happens by phone and by email, into a shared inbox that Natalie Fairweather's team has to triage by hand. Claims get lost in that inbox. A partner who submitted a claim three weeks ago has no way to check whether anyone has even looked at it yet, short of calling and asking. And a growing number of those 200 partners run their own field-service software -- scheduling tools, mobile apps their technicians use in the field -- with no way to talk to Brindlewood's systems at all.

You are **Dmitri Kowalski**, the ServiceNow Developer who's going to build the real fix. This video starts where a responsible build like this has to start: in a room with the person who owns this problem, before a single scoped application exists.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine 200 different repair shops all over the country fix the same brand of washing machine, and whenever they fix one that's still under warranty, they have to mail a letter to the washing machine company to get paid for the repair. All 200 shops mail their letters to the same mailbox. Someone at the washing machine company has to open every single letter by hand, figure out what it's about, and write back -- and sometimes a letter gets stuck at the bottom of the pile, or falls behind the mailbox, and nobody notices for weeks. The repair shop that sent it has no way to peek inside the mailbox and see if their letter even made it, so they just call and ask, over and over.

Some of those repair shops also have their own computer systems that track their repairs automatically. Right now those computers can't talk to the washing machine company's computers at all -- a person still has to write a letter by hand even if a computer already knows everything that letter needs to say.

Brindlewood Industrial has exactly this problem, except it's warranty claims instead of washing machines, and the mailbox is a shared email inbox. Before Dmitri builds anything, he has to sit down with the person in charge and really understand how bad the mailbox problem actually is.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail worth getting precise about in this discovery meeting is not "partners need a better way to submit claims" -- that much is obvious from a single conversation with anyone on Natalie Fairweather's team. What's worth getting precise about is the three distinct failure modes hiding inside "a shared inbox," because each one points toward a different piece of the eventual solution, and conflating them leads to building the wrong thing well.

First, there's **loss and triage cost**: claims genuinely get missed or delayed because a shared inbox has no structured queue, no required fields, and no way to tell at a glance what's new versus what's already being worked. Second, there's **status invisibility**: once a partner sends a claim, they have no self-service way to check where it stands -- every status check becomes a phone call or a reply-all email thread, which is real, recurring work for Natalie's team that a self-service view would eliminate entirely. Third, and the one that's easy to under-weight in a first conversation, is **the integration gap**: a meaningful number of Brindlewood's 200 partners already run their own field-service management software, and that software has no way to create or check a Brindlewood warranty claim programmatically. A partner-facing web portal solves the first two problems for a human looking at a screen. It does nothing for a partner's own software trying to talk to Brindlewood's systems -- that gap needs a real API, not just a nicer form.

Four people matter in this build, and it's worth meeting all of them in this first conversation rather than discovering their constraints later. **Natalie Fairweather**, Director of Partner Operations, is the business sponsor -- she wants partners to self-serve both submission and status, and just as importantly, she wants her own team out of the business of triaging a shared inbox by hand. **Dmitri Kowalski** is the developer who will build the scoped application, the portal, and the API. **Zara Ahmed**, ServiceNow Technical Architect, will run a pre-launch security review before this goes anywhere near 200 external partner accounts -- establishing that review as a real, scheduled gate now, rather than inventing it under deadline pressure later, matters because this application will hold data from partners who, in some local markets, directly compete with each other. **Owen Castellano**, ServiceNow Platform Administrator, supports the platform-level configuration this scoped application will need to live inside -- access control lists, instance settings, and how a new scope coexists with everything Brindlewood already runs on the platform.

Getting the real shape of the problem right now -- lost claims, invisible status, and a closed door to partners' own software -- is what keeps every requirement written in the next lesson honest about what Brindlewood actually needs, instead of what simply sounds like a reasonable portal project in isolation.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in with real questions, not assumptions

Before the meeting, write down what you need to confirm, not what you expect to hear:

- How many claims actually move through the shared inbox in a typical month, and how many of Natalie's people spend real time triaging it?
- Do partners already have any kind of login to a Brindlewood system today, for anything?
- How many of the 200 partners run their own field-service software, and does anyone actually know what "integration" would mean to them?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real ask in Natalie Fairweather's own words

```
NATALIE:   Here's the real problem. We have about 200 partners doing
           warranty repairs on our equipment in the field, and every
           single claim comes in by phone or email, into one shared
           inbox my team has to sort by hand. Claims get buried.
           Partners call us constantly just to ask "did you get my
           claim?" because they have no way to check themselves.

DMITRI:    And what happens on the partner side when their claim
           just sits there?

NATALIE:   They have no visibility at all. Some of them run their
           own scheduling and field-service software, and they've
           asked outright whether that software can just talk to us
           directly instead of someone typing an email. Right now
           the honest answer is no -- there's nothing for it to talk
           to.
```

## Step 3 -- Ask Zara Ahmed what has to be true before 200 outside companies get access

```
DMITRI:    Zara, before any of this goes live with real partner
           accounts, what does your side look like?

ZARA:      A real security review before launch -- not a formality.
           Remember, a lot of these 200 partners compete directly
           with each other in the same local markets. If one
           partner's account could ever see another partner's
           claims, that's not a bug ticket, that's a trust failure
           we don't get to walk back. I'll check that properly once
           there's something real to review.

DMITRI:    Good to hear that now, before I've designed anything
           around an assumption that isn't actually verified yet.
```

## Step 4 -- Ask Owen Castellano what he needs to know about the platform

```
DMITRI:    Owen, what do you need to know as this gets built?

OWEN:      Whatever this is, it needs to live cleanly alongside
           everything else already running on this instance --
           don't touch global configuration if a scoped application
           can do the job instead. And loop me in early on access
           control and instance-level settings; that's platform
           work, not application work, and I'd rather plan for it
           than find out about it after the fact.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm the real shape of the problem

```
BRINDLEWOOD'S WARRANTY CLAIM PROBLEM -- WHAT NATALIE IS ACTUALLY DESCRIBING

Failure mode              What happens today              Who feels it
Claims get lost           Shared inbox, no structured      Natalie's team
                          queue, manual triage              + partners
Status is invisible       No way for a partner to check    Partners
                          their own claim's status
No programmatic access    Partners' own field-service       Partners'
                          software can't create or check    own software
                          claims

Rough shape of a fix (not yet decided in detail):
  - A proper structured place to track a claim, not an inbox.
  - A partner-facing self-service view of claim status.
  - A way for partners' own software to reach Brindlewood
    programmatically, not just a nicer web form.
```

```

lessons.title: Turning 'Partners Need Self-Service' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Natalie Fairweather's 'partners need self-service' into one precise, testable requirement: every partner must be able to submit and track their own claims through the portal AND through the API, and must never be able to see another partner's claims through either path -- the API included from the start, not an afterthought.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and an honest picture of what Brindlewood actually needs -- but "partners need self-service" isn't a requirement yet, it's a direction. This lesson turns that direction into one precise, written requirement you can actually design against and, eventually, test.

The requirement has two halves that have to be stated together, because treating them separately is exactly how a project like this goes wrong. First, every one of Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners must be able to submit a new warranty claim and check the status of their own existing claims through **both** a self-service portal **and** a Scripted REST API -- the API is not a nice-to-have bolted on after the portal ships, it's named as equally in-scope from this requirement's first draft, because that's the only way a partner's own field-service software can realistically participate. Second, and inseparably, a partner must **never** be able to see another partner's claims through **either** path -- not through the portal, and not through the API. Whether the finished system actually lives up to that second half is something this series has to verify honestly later, through Zara Ahmed's security review, not something to assume is true just because an access control list exists somewhere in the design. Whether partners will actually only ever see their own data, everywhere, not just in the portal, stays the open question driving the rest of this series.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the school finally agrees to build a real set of mailboxes for the 200 repair shops instead of one shared mailbox. "Give everyone their own mailbox" doesn't tell anyone exactly what to build. So they get specific: every repair shop needs a key that opens only their own mailbox slot, whether they walk up and check it in person, or send their own little robot to check it for them. And just as important: shop A's key must never open shop B's slot -- not when a person tries it, and not when shop B's robot tries it either. It would do no good at all to build great individual mailboxes for people, and then leave the robots able to reach into anyone's slot because nobody thought to check.

That's the requirement for Brindlewood. Partners have to be able to create and check their own claims, whether a person is clicking around a website or their own computer system is checking in automatically -- and no partner, through either door, ever gets to see another partner's claims.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that only describes the happy path for one access method isn't a complete requirement -- it's half of one, and the missing half is usually where the real risk lives. "Partners need self-service" is easy to satisfy on paper by shipping a portal where a logged-in partner sees only their own claims. That's necessary, but it quietly leaves the API as an unstated, unscoped afterthought -- exactly the gap that tends to get built last, tested least, and reviewed least carefully, because nobody wrote down on day one that it carries the same stakes as the UI.

This requirement closes that gap by naming both access paths together, as one requirement, not two. REQ-1 states that every partner must be able to create a claim and query claim status through the self-service portal, and REQ-2 states that every partner must be able to do the same two things through a Scripted REST API intended for partners' own field-service software -- stated side by side specifically so neither one is treated as secondary to the other. REQ-3 is the requirement that actually protects Brindlewood and its partners from the failure that matters most: a partner must never be able to retrieve or view another partner's claim data, through the portal or through the API, under any request. Because Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners are frequently direct local competitors, a cross-partner data leak isn't a cosmetic bug -- it's the kind of trust failure Natalie Fairweather and Zara Ahmed both flagged in discovery as the real stakes of this build.

This lesson does not yet claim that the system, once built, actually satisfies REQ-3 across every access path. It commits Brindlewood, in writing, to a standard that has to be verified honestly once the application, the ACL, the portal, and the API all actually exist -- including verifying the API path specifically, rather than assuming that an access control list which correctly protects the portal's UI automatically protects every other way of reaching the same table.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Natalie's side of the business

```
DMITRI:    You said partners need self-service. What would actually
           have to be true for you to call that delivered?

NATALIE:   Two things, really. Every partner needs to be able to
           submit a claim and check on it themselves -- whether
           they're clicking through a website, or their own
           field-service software is doing it for them
           automatically. And no partner should ever be able to see
           another partner's claims. Some of these partners compete
           with each other in the same city. If partner A could ever
           see partner B's warranty claims, that's a real problem for
           us, not a minor glitch.

DMITRI:    Can I push on the second part? Does that need to hold for
           the portal, or for every way a claim can be reached?

NATALIE:   Every way. I don't want to find out later that the
           website was fine but something else wasn't.
```

## Step 2 -- Ask Zara Ahmed what verifying that actually requires

```
DMITRI:    Zara, if the requirement is "never see another partner's
           claims, anywhere," what does checking that really mean?

ZARA:      It means checking every door into that data, not just the
           front door. A row-level ACL on the claims table is the
           right mechanism, but an ACL that's correctly enforced for
           the portal doesn't automatically prove it's enforced for
           an API endpoint that touches the same table -- those are
           two different code paths, and I'll be checking both before
           this goes anywhere near 200 real partner accounts.

DMITRI:    That's exactly why I want the API named in this
           requirement now, not added quietly later.
```

## Step 3 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

```
REQUIREMENT -- PARTNER SELF-SERVICE (V1)

REQ-1: Every partner must be able to submit a new warranty claim and
       check the status of their own existing claims through a
       partner-facing self-service portal.
REQ-2: Every partner must be able to do the same two things --
       create a claim and query claim status -- through a Scripted
       REST API, so a partner's own field-service software can
       participate without a human using the portal.
REQ-3: A partner must never be able to view or retrieve another
       partner's claim data, through the portal or through the API,
       under any request. This is a hard requirement, not a
       best-effort goal, and it must be verified across both access
       paths, not assumed from one.
```

## Step 4 -- Say out loud what this requirement doesn't promise yet

```
DMITRI:    I want to be clear about one thing. REQ-1 through REQ-3
           are the standard we're building toward. They're not yet a
           claim that the finished system actually meets that
           standard on every path. That's real design and build work
           ahead, and Zara's review is where we find out honestly,
           not something I get to assume because the requirement
           reads well on paper.

NATALIE:   Fair -- I just need to know that's genuinely the bar, and
           that someone checks it before real partner accounts touch
           this.
```

## Step 5 -- Sanity-check the requirement against a real scenario

```
Scenario: Partner A's field-service software calls the Scripted REST
          API to check the status of a claim, but passes a claim
          number that actually belongs to Partner B. Under REQ-3,
          that request must be denied or return nothing -- the same
          outcome a browser would get trying the portal with Partner
          A's own login. If the API instead returns Partner B's
          claim data because the API itself doesn't enforce the same
          restriction the portal does, that is exactly the failure
          REQ-3 exists to prevent.
```

Walk this scenario past Natalie Fairweather and Zara Ahmed directly and ask: "Is this exactly what you mean by partners never seeing each other's claims?"

## Step 6 -- Get the requirement signed off

Save REQ-1 through REQ-3 alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Natalie Fairweather on REQ-3 specifically -- the requirement that it holds across both the portal and the API, not just the one that's easiest to see working in a demo, is the line most likely to get quietly assumed rather than actually verified once a launch date is close.

REQ-3 explicitly requires verification across both access paths, not an assumption carried over from the portal alone.

Natalie has signed off in writing, which is what every later design and build decision in this project gets measured against.

Because many of our partners compete with each other locally, that second part is treated as a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: One Scoped App, One API -- Not a Portal Rebuild
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- the Warranty Claim scoped application, its ACL, the partner portal, Flow Designer automation, and the Scripted REST API -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: automated parts-ordering, Brindlewood's broader customer-facing website, and self-service for Brindlewood's own internal employees.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any configuration happens in ServiceNow, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this build actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Brindlewood Industrial, V1 ships five things: the **Partner Warranty Claims** scoped application itself (internal scope name `x_brind_claims`); its custom `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` table and the row-level ACL that enforces REQ-3 on it; a partner-facing self-service portal built on the Service Portal or a simple UI page; Flow Designer automation that routes new claims and notifies the right internal reviewer; and a Scripted REST API, also in the `x_brind_claims` scope, that lets partners' own field-service software create and query claims.

What's explicitly out of scope, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond that warranty-claim core. This project does not build **automated parts-ordering or inventory integration** -- a real, named V2 idea that would let an approved claim automatically trigger a parts order, deliberately deferred rather than quietly dropped. It does not rebuild **Brindlewood's broader customer-facing website** -- that's a different system entirely, not something this scoped application touches. And it does not extend self-service claim access to **Brindlewood's own internal employees** -- V1 is partners only; any internal employee experience for warranty claims is a separate, later conversation.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the school finally gets real help building the mailbox system for the 200 repair shops. A good helper does one job well: build real mailboxes, give everyone the right key, and make sure robots and people both only reach their own slot. A helper who also tried to build a whole new general store at the same time, or started automatically reordering supplies every time a mailbox got a letter, or tried to give the school's own kids mailboxes too, before the first 200 mailboxes even worked properly -- that helper is doing a much bigger job than anyone actually asked for, and the one thing that really matters right now might never get finished well.

Brindlewood's project is the helper doing the first job well. It builds the claim mailboxes for the 200 outside partners, tests the keys carefully, and stops there -- it doesn't also try to build a parts-ordering robot or a brand-new website or mailboxes for Brindlewood's own employees at the same time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working claims system is an unusually tempting foundation to build on top of once it exists. The moment claims are flowing cleanly through a structured table instead of an inbox, it's natural for stakeholders to ask "can approved claims also trigger a parts order automatically?" or "can we put this same self-service experience in front of our own internal warranty team?" Both are reasonable product ideas, and neither belongs in V1.

Automated parts-ordering and inventory integration are deferred because they're a genuinely separate problem with their own integration surface -- connecting claim approval to Brindlewood's parts and inventory systems means new data contracts, new failure modes (what happens when a part is out of stock, or an order fails partway through), and its own testing and review, independent of whether claim submission and status-tracking themselves work correctly. Bundling that into V1 means two different kinds of risk sharing one launch date, which serves neither well -- it's named now specifically so it has a real place to resurface as V2, rather than getting silently dropped or, worse, rushed into V1 under scope pressure.

Rebuilding Brindlewood's broader customer-facing website is out of scope for the clearest reason of all: it's an entirely different system, serving an entirely different audience (Brindlewood's own customers, not its 200 service partners), with its own ownership and its own release cadence -- there's no reason for a scoped ServiceNow application built for partner warranty claims to touch it at all.

And extending this self-service experience to Brindlewood's own internal employees is deferred for a reason worth stating precisely: REQ-3's hard partner-isolation requirement was designed and will be verified against partner accounts and partner-to-partner data boundaries specifically. Internal employees have a different relationship to this data entirely -- an internal reviewer may legitimately need to see claims across multiple partners as part of their job, which is a different access model than REQ-3's partner-to-partner isolation, not a smaller version of it. Folding that in now, under the same ACL design built for a different access pattern, risks getting both models wrong. V1 commits to something narrower and fully ownable: one scoped application, one ACL, one portal, one API, built and verified for partners -- not a parts-ordering integration, not a website rebuild, and not an internal-employee experience layered on top before the partner-facing core is proven.

That's the line most likely to get reinterpreted later, once a working partner portal exists and looks easy to extend to other audiences.

## Step 6 -- Treat the deferred list as a real backlog, not a dead end

Naming parts-ordering integration and internal-employee access as deferred, rather than simply declining them, matters for how the rest of the organization reads this decision. A deferred item has an owner, a rough rationale, and a place it can resurface once V1 has actually shipped and proven itself; a silently dropped idea tends to come back later as a surprise, re-argued from scratch, often at a worse time. Dmitri keeps both items in the same written record as the V1 scope statement, specifically so that when the warehouse team raises parts-ordering again in six months, the answer is "yes, that's still on the list, here's why it waited," not a blank look.

Automated parts-ordering/inventory integration, a rebuild of the customer-facing website, and internal-employee self-service are all explicitly out of scope and named as separate, deferred items.

lessons.title: Choosing the Approach: A Scoped App and a Scripted REST API
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: building Partner Warranty Claims as a scoped application rather than in the global scope, and building a real Scripted REST API rather than relying on the portal alone -- each justified against a real alternative for Brindlewood's actual situation.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly how Partner Warranty Claims gets built on the ServiceNow platform. This lesson fixes two choices. First, the application is built as a **scoped application** (`x_brind_claims`), not configured directly in the global scope. Second, partners get a real **Scripted REST API**, in that same `x_brind_claims` scope, in addition to -- not instead of -- the self-service portal.

Each choice earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. Building in the global scope was a real option Owen Castellano would have had to live with, and it's rejected for a specific reason: Brindlewood already has other customizations running on this instance, and a scoped application keeps Partner Warranty Claims' tables, business logic, and ACLs isolated from all of that, so a change made inside `x_brind_claims` can't accidentally break something unrelated, and vice versa. Relying on the portal alone, without a real API, was the other real option, and it's rejected because it would fail REQ-2 outright: partners' own field-service software can click nothing and fill out no form -- it needs an actual programmatic interface to create and query claims, which only a real API provides. This lesson fixes the approach. It does not yet claim that building it this way alone guarantees REQ-3 holds across both the portal and the API -- that depends on how the ACL, the table, and the API are each actually built and verified, which is real work still ahead in this series, not something to assume solved just because the right architectural shape was chosen.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the school is finally building the real mailbox system, and has to decide two things: where to build it, and how shops can check their mail.

First, where to build it. The school could bolt the new mailboxes onto the exact same wall as every other club's bulletin board and supply closet, where one mistake while hanging a mailbox could knock someone else's stuff down too. Or they could build the mailboxes on their own separate, clearly labeled wall, so nothing anyone does there can mess up anyone else's stuff, and nothing anyone else does can mess up the mailboxes. The separate wall is the better choice, because this school already has plenty of other things going on, on other walls.

Second, how shops check their mail. If the only way to check is walking up to the mailbox wall in person and looking at it, that's fine for a shop owner, but useless for a shop's own little robot that's supposed to check automatically every morning. A robot can't walk up and read a mailbox label -- it needs its own special slot it knows how to talk to. So the school builds both: the wall you can walk up to, and a robot-friendly slot that works the exact same way, every time, for any robot that knows how to use it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Both decisions here trace back to a real constraint from the earlier lessons, not a default configuration choice.

Start with **scoped application versus global scope**. Brindlewood's ServiceNow instance already carries other customizations -- Owen Castellano's concern in discovery was explicitly that whatever gets built here needs to coexist cleanly with everything else already running. A scoped application gives `x_brind_claims` its own namespace for tables, business rules, ACLs, and script includes, with application access controls governing what code inside the scope can reach outside it and vice versa. That isolation is the real reason this choice wins here: it means a mistake in a `x_brind_claims` business rule can't silently corrupt an unrelated table elsewhere on the instance, and a future change to something unrelated on the instance can't silently break Partner Warranty Claims. Building this directly in the global scope was a real option -- global-scope customizations are simpler to wire together in some respects -- but it trades away exactly the isolation Owen flagged as a real concern, for a benefit this project doesn't actually need.

The decision that deserves the most scrutiny is **building a real Scripted REST API rather than relying on the self-service portal alone**. It would be entirely possible to satisfy REQ-1 with just a well-built Service Portal widget, and stop there -- plenty of self-service projects do exactly that, because most of their users are humans clicking through a browser. Brindlewood's situation is different in a way that was named explicitly in discovery: a meaningful number of its 200 partners already run their own field-service management software, and REQ-2 commits, in writing, to letting that software create and query claims programmatically. A portal, no matter how well designed, is built for a human looking at a screen -- it has no answer for a partner's own backend system trying to post a new claim at 2 a.m. when a technician logs a repair. A Scripted REST API, built in the `x_brind_claims` scope alongside the application's own tables and business logic, is the only piece of this architecture that actually gives partners' software something to call. Choosing to build it now, as a first-class part of V1 rather than a maybe-later addition, is what keeps REQ-2 from becoming the requirement that quietly never gets built once the portal looks like it's working fine on its own.

Neither decision, on its own, proves REQ-3 holds everywhere. A scoped application and a real API are the right shape for this problem -- whether the ACL on `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` is actually enforced correctly across both the portal and the API is a question the implementation and Zara Ahmed's security review still have to answer honestly, not something this architectural choice gets to claim credit for in advance.

lessons.title: Designing the Warranty Claim Table and Partner Data Model
lessons.summary: Designing the x_brind_claims_warranty_claim table's seven fields and, more importantly, how its partner_company field ties every claim back to the Company record Brindlewood already keeps for that partner -- settling the data model before Dmitri creates a single field in Studio.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the scoped-application-plus-API approach locked in the last lesson, this lesson does the one piece of design work everything else in this series depends on: deciding exactly what a Warranty Claim record has to hold, and how it identifies which of Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners it belongs to.

The table itself -- label "Warranty Claim", table name `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` -- needs seven fields: `partner_company`, `equipment_serial`, `issue_description`, `state`, `labor_hours`, `parts_cost`, and `resolution_notes`. Six of those are straightforward. The seventh, `partner_company`, is the one that matters most, because it's the field every later piece of this build -- the access rule in the next lesson, the portal, the API -- will ultimately depend on to answer one question correctly: whose claim is this?

Dmitri isn't inventing a new way to represent "partner" from scratch. Brindlewood already tracks its roughly 200 authorized service partners somewhere on the platform -- as Company records -- and this lesson's real design decision is to reuse that existing identity rather than build a second, parallel notion of "partner" that could drift out of sync with the first. This lesson settles the field list and that reference relationship. No table, no field, and no choice list actually gets created in Studio until lesson 8.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine Brindlewood already keeps a drawer of index cards, one card per outside repair shop it works with -- shop name, address, all the basic facts. Now Dmitri has to design a new kind of card: a warranty claim card. Before he prints a single one, he has to decide exactly what blanks go on it -- which equipment, what's wrong with it, how many labor hours, how much the parts cost, notes on how it got resolved -- and, most importantly, how the claim card points back to the right shop's card in that existing drawer.

The easy wrong way to do this is to just write the shop's name on the claim card by hand. Someone could misspell it, or two shops could have similar names, and now nobody's sure whose claim is whose. The right way -- the way Dmitri designs it -- is for the claim card to clip directly onto the shop's actual card in the drawer, so there's never any doubt. This lesson is drawing that design on paper. The actual cards don't get printed yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The six "ordinary" fields are worth naming precisely because the choices made for them aren't arbitrary: `equipment_serial` as a string (free-text, since serial number formats vary by equipment line and Brindlewood doesn't need to validate format at this layer), `issue_description` and `resolution_notes` as multi-line text (a single-line string would truncate exactly the kind of detail a reviewer needs to approve or deny a claim), `state` as a choice field with five fixed values -- New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed -- rather than free text, so that every downstream piece of this build (the routing automation two lessons from now, any report Natalie's team runs) can rely on a closed, known set of values instead of parsing whatever string happened to get typed in. `labor_hours` as a decimal and `parts_cost` as a currency field are chosen specifically because they're the two numbers this claim exists to produce -- what Brindlewood ultimately reimburses the partner for -- and currency fields carry their own formatting and multi-currency handling that a plain decimal wouldn't give for free.

`partner_company` is the field that deserves the real scrutiny. The design decision is to make it a reference field pointing at the platform's own Company table (`core_company`) -- the same table Brindlewood already uses to represent every organization it does business with, partners included -- rather than inventing a bespoke `x_brind_claims_partner` table that duplicates identity Brindlewood already has. Reusing `core_company` means a claim's partner is never a loose string that can drift out of sync with reality; it's a direct pointer to one specific, already-governed record.

That reference relationship matters for a second reason that reaches well past this one table. Every one of Brindlewood's roughly 200 partner contacts who gets a ServiceNow account to use the eventual self-service portal will have that account's standard `sys_user.company` field set to their own partner's Company record -- that's how a partner's login is tied to their organization in the first place, and setting it correctly is Owen Castellano's responsibility during account provisioning, not something this scoped application has to invent. Designing `partner_company` as a reference to the exact same Company table that `sys_user.company` already points to is what makes it possible, later, to compare "whose claim is this" against "who's logged in" as a direct, reliable match between two references to the same record -- rather than comparing two different representations of "partner" that happen to mean the same thing today and might not tomorrow. This lesson settles that it's the same table on both sides. It does not yet decide how, where, or by what mechanism that comparison actually gets enforced -- that's the next lesson's job, and the literal build is two lessons further out.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Start from what a claim actually has to record

Dmitri starts from Natalie Fairweather's own description of a warranty claim, not from a generic template: a partner reports which piece of equipment they repaired, what was wrong with it, how many labor hours they spent, what the parts cost, and -- once Brindlewood's reviewer has looked at it -- notes on how it was resolved and where it currently stands. That's six of the seven fields, directly off the real business problem.

## Step 2 -- Decide what "whose claim is this" actually means

The seventh field, `partner_company`, is the one Dmitri spends the most time on. Brindlewood already represents every one of its roughly 200 authorized service partners as a Company record on the platform. The decision: `partner_company` is a reference field pointing at that same Company table (`core_company`), not a new, separate partner table and not a plain text field holding a company name.

```
Decision: partner_company references Company [core_company]
Alternative considered: a new, dedicated x_brind_claims_partner table
Why the reference wins: Brindlewood already has governed partner
  identity in core_company. A separate table would duplicate it and
  could drift out of sync. A reference keeps one source of truth.
```

## Step 3 -- Fix the field list

```
FIELD              TYPE                 PURPOSE
partner_company    Reference            Which partner filed this claim --
                    (Company/core_company) points at Brindlewood's existing
                                          Company record for that partner.
equipment_serial   String               Serial number of the repaired unit.
issue_description  Multi-line text      What the partner found wrong.
state               Choice               New / In Review / Approved /
                                          Denied / Closed.
labor_hours         Decimal              Hours billed for the repair.
parts_cost          Currency             Cost of parts used, for
                                          reimbursement.
resolution_notes    Multi-line text      Reviewer's notes on how the
                                          claim was closed out.
```

## Step 4 -- Design the state choice list

The five values are fixed in order, with New as the required starting point for every claim:

```
1. New          -- just submitted, nobody has looked at it yet
2. In Review    -- an internal reviewer is actively working it
3. Approved     -- reimbursement approved
4. Denied       -- claim rejected
5. Closed       -- fully resolved, no further action
```

## Step 5 -- Decide why labor_hours and parts_cost need their own types

`labor_hours` is a decimal rather than an integer, since partial hours are routine in field service. `parts_cost` is a currency field rather than a plain decimal specifically because it needs to carry proper currency formatting -- this is the number Brindlewood ultimately reimburses, and it should render and store like money, not like an arbitrary number.

## Step 6 -- Confirm the design and name what's still open

Dmitri walks this field list and the `partner_company` reference decision past Natalie Fairweather and Zara Ahmed.

```
DMITRI:    Every claim points directly at the partner's existing
           Company record -- the same one their portal login will
           eventually be tied to. That's deliberate: there's only
           ever one place that says who a partner actually is.

ZARA:      Good. I'll want that confirmed again once there's an
           access rule sitting on top of it -- but as a data model,
           reusing core_company instead of inventing something new
           is the right call.
```

This lesson settles the field list and the `partner_company` relationship only. How a future rule will compare a claim's `partner_company` to a logged-in user is the next lesson's planning work. The literal table and its fields get created in Studio in lesson 8, not here.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Settled the Warranty Claim data model: seven fields on x_brind_claims_warranty_claim, with partner_company as a Reference to the existing Company [core_company] table rather than a new partner table -- the same table sys_user.company already points to for each partner's own login. State is a five-value choice (New/In Review/Approved/Denied/Closed). No table or field exists yet; this is the design only.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've settled exactly what information a warranty claim needs to capture and, critically, how each claim will tie back to the correct partner using records we already maintain, rather than building a second, separate way of identifying partners. Nothing is built yet -- this is the design the real table gets built from in a later lesson.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've designed the data structure for tracking warranty claims, making sure each claim is tied cleanly to the correct partner using our existing partner records rather than creating a new, potentially inconsistent way of identifying who's who. This is design work only -- the actual system gets built in a later step.

lessons.title: Planning the ACL and Multi-Tenant Access Model
lessons.summary: Planning the row-level security rule for Warranty Claim -- every partner restricted to their own company's claims -- and fixing the principle that this isolation has to hold everywhere the table can be reached, not just through whichever path is easiest to demo, before any ACL actually gets written.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
REQ-3, signed off back in lesson 2, says a partner must never see another partner's claims, through the portal or the API. This lesson is where that requirement starts turning into an actual security design for `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` -- not the finished rule itself, which is a dedicated build lesson still ahead, but the plan Zara Ahmed and Dmitri agree on before either one touches an access control list.

The plan has two parts. The first is the rule itself, stated in plain language: a user should only be able to read, and act on, a Warranty Claim record whose `partner_company` matches their own company -- the same `sys_user.company` field lesson 5's design already settled as the anchor on the partner side. The second part is the harder one, and it's the part this lesson spends the most time on: naming, explicitly, every distinct way this table's data can end up in front of someone, and committing that the isolation rule has to hold for all of them, not just the one that's easiest to click through in a demo. Nothing gets built in this lesson. The row-level ACL itself is a dedicated build lesson immediately ahead.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a locker room where every locker has a combination lock, and the rule is simple: your combination only opens your own locker. That rule has to be true no matter how someone tries a locker -- whether they walk up and spin the dial themselves, or they send someone else to try it for them with their combination written on a card. A locker room that only checks the rule when someone walks up in person, but forgets to check it when a note gets handed through a side window, doesn't actually have the rule at all -- it just looks like it does, until someone tries the side window.

Zara and Dmitri are planning Brindlewood's version of that lock: one rule -- your company's claims are the only claims you can see -- and a promise to check, carefully, that the rule actually holds at every single door into the room, not just the front one. They're not installing the lock yet. They're agreeing on exactly what it has to do and exactly how thoroughly it has to be tested, everywhere.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The security mechanism Zara settles on at the planning level is a row-level ACL on `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`: a server-side condition, evaluated against the specific record being accessed and the logged-in user's own record, that only grants access when the claim's `partner_company` equals the requesting user's company. That's the standard ServiceNow pattern for exactly this shape of problem -- a table that holds records belonging to different external organizations, where each organization's users must be confined to their own -- and it's deliberately a server-enforced condition on the table itself, not a filter applied by whatever UI happens to be displaying the data, precisely because a condition owned by the table is the only version of this rule that every consumer of the table is supposed to inherit automatically.

"Supposed to" is the exact phrase this lesson spends its time on. Zara is explicit with Dmitri that a correctly written ACL protects every access path that goes through the platform's normal data-access layer -- list views, form views, and anything built against the table the standard way, including reports and Service Portal widgets that read records through the ordinary APIs those tools use. What an ACL does not do automatically is protect a path that was built to reach the table's data by some other route -- and Brindlewood's planned Scripted REST API is exactly the kind of component that gets to choose its own route to the data, because it's custom server-side script, not a standard UI component consuming the table the ordinary way. This lesson does not decide, and is not the place to decide, how the eventual API will be written, or whether its implementation will or won't end up going through the same enforcement the portal gets for free. That's real implementation work for the lesson that actually builds the API, further ahead in this series. What this lesson fixes now is the standard the implementation has to be checked against once it exists: the isolation rule is one rule, and it has to be verified -- independently, access path by access path -- rather than assumed to follow automatically just because it holds for the path that's easiest to click through.

Zara states the plan to Dmitri directly: once the ACL, the portal, and eventually the API all exist, she will test each access path on its own terms -- try to read another partner's claim through the portal as a logged-in partner user, and separately, once it exists, try to read another partner's claim through whatever interface the API presents -- rather than testing one path, finding it clean, and letting that stand in for the rest. That verification doesn't happen in this lesson. What gets fixed here is the commitment to do it that way, and the plain statement of the single rule everything downstream gets measured against.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Restate REQ-3 in Zara's own terms

```
ZARA:      REQ-3 says a partner never sees another partner's claims,
           through the portal or the API. I want to plan the actual
           mechanism for that now, before the table has any data in
           it worth protecting.

DMITRI:    The data model's already set up for it -- partner_company
           on the claim, company on the partner's own user account,
           same Company table on both sides.
```

## Step 2 -- State the rule in plain language

```
THE RULE (planning level, not yet a built ACL):
  A user may read or act on a Warranty Claim record only when that
  record's partner_company matches the requesting user's own
  company.
```

## Step 3 -- Name every distinct door into this table's data

This is the step Zara insists on doing carefully, in writing, rather than assuming:

```
ACCESS PATH                         MUST HONOR THE RULE?
Self-service portal (partner view)   Yes
Internal list/form views (reviewers) Yes -- reviewers see claims
                                      across partners by role, a
                                      different, intentional
                                      exception -- not a gap.
Reports built against this table     Yes
Any future way of reaching this      Yes -- including the planned
  table's data programmatically       Scripted REST API, once built.
```

## Step 4 -- Fix the principle driving the rest of this series

```
ZARA:      A standard ACL on the table protects everything that goes
           through the platform's normal access layer -- forms,
           lists, reports, portal widgets built the ordinary way.
           What it doesn't protect automatically is anything custom
           that chooses its own route to the same data. The API is
           exactly that kind of component.

DMITRI:    So the rule is one rule, but it isn't automatically true
           everywhere just because it's true somewhere.

ZARA:      Right. And I'm not deciding today how the API will be
           built to respect it -- that's real work for whoever
           writes it. What I'm fixing today is that it has to be,
           and that I check it myself once it exists.
```

## Step 5 -- Agree on how this gets verified later, not now

Zara commits to testing each access path independently once it exists: log in as one partner, attempt to reach another partner's claim through the portal, confirm it's blocked; separately, once the API exists, attempt the same thing through whatever interface it presents. Neither test is run in this lesson -- there's no ACL and no API yet to test against.

## Step 6 -- Name what's deliberately not decided yet

```
Settled in this lesson:
  - The rule itself: partner_company must match the user's company.
  - The principle: it must hold on every access path, verified
    independently, not assumed from one path to the next.

Deliberately not decided here:
  - The literal ACL script, its operations, and its roles -- a
    dedicated build lesson, immediately ahead.
  - How the planned Scripted REST API's implementation will be
    built to respect this same rule -- a decision for the lesson
    that writes it, further ahead in this series.
```

No ACL exists yet; this is the plan and its verification standard only.

Nothing is built yet; this sets the bar the real security work gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've locked in the security principle that protects our partners' confidentiality from each other: each partner only ever sees their own claims, and that has to be true everywhere our systems can be reached, not just on the obvious screen. This is the standard we're building toward -- the actual safeguard gets built and tested in the steps ahead.

lessons.title: Planning Integration, Automation, and Testing Strategy
lessons.summary: Planning the Flow Designer automation that routes a new claim to the right internal reviewer, the purpose and endpoint shape of the Scripted REST API partners' field-service software will call, and a two-phase testing strategy -- ATF coverage plus a pre-launch UAT phase with real partner accounts -- before any of it gets implemented.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Three pieces of V1 haven't been planned yet, and this lesson plans all three before implementation starts in earnest: the Flow Designer automation that moves a new claim from "just submitted" to "in front of the right person at Brindlewood," the Scripted REST API's purpose and the specific endpoints partners' own field-service software will actually call, and the testing strategy that has to clear before any of it reaches a real partner account.

None of this gets built in this lesson. Dmitri plans the automation's trigger and actions with Natalie Fairweather's routing needs in mind, plans the API's shape -- what it's for and which operations it exposes -- without yet deciding the implementation details of how it enforces REQ-3 (that's real work for the lesson that actually writes it), and plans a testing approach with Zara Ahmed that treats an automated test suite and a hands-on rehearsal with real partners as two different, both-necessary kinds of proof.

Three things get planned today, on paper, before any of them actually gets built.

First, think of a mail room that used to just pile letters on one desk. Now there's a plan for a conveyor belt: a new letter drops onto it, the belt reads who it's for, and it lands on the right desk with a little flag raised so that person notices it. That's the claim-routing automation.

Second, think about adding a drive-through window to the side of a building that only ever had a walk-in counter. The plan says what that window is for -- outside delivery trucks pulling up and dropping something off or asking a quick question, without a person needing to walk in -- and roughly what they'll be allowed to ask for. It doesn't yet say exactly how the person working the window checks whose delivery is whose; that's a real question, just not today's question.

Third, before any of this opens for real, there's a plan for two different kinds of practice run: a checklist a robot can run every single day to make sure the basics still work, and a dress rehearsal with a handful of actual outside partners, acting like real customers, before the doors open to everyone.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The Flow Designer plan is straightforward and specific: a flow triggered on record creation on `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` where `state` is New, which determines the appropriate internal reviewer -- Natalie's team needs to confirm whether that's a flat queue, routing by equipment type, or round-robin assignment, which is a detail this lesson flags as still open with her -- sets the claim's `state` to In Review, and fires a notification to that reviewer. The flow's job stops there; what a reviewer does once notified (approve, deny, request more information) is form-level work a reviewer performs directly on the record, not something this automation decides on their behalf.

The Scripted REST API plan fixes purpose and shape without fixing implementation. Purpose: give a partner's own field-service software a way to create a new claim and check the status of claims that partner has already submitted, without a human filling out the portal. Planned endpoints, at the resource level: a create operation that accepts the same fields a partner would enter in the portal, a status-lookup operation for a single claim, and a list operation returning that partner's own claims. What this lesson does not decide is how the API establishes which partner is calling on a given request, or how its implementation will be built to respect the same isolation rule planned in the last lesson -- both are real decisions for the lesson that writes the API, not settled in advance here. It's a reasonable, deliberate gap at this stage: the API's authentication approach and its data-access implementation are build-time decisions, not planning-time ones, and naming them as open rather than guessing at them now keeps this plan honest about what it has and hasn't actually settled.

The testing plan has two tiers, and Zara is explicit that neither one substitutes for the other. The Automated Test Framework (ATF) suite is planned to run against every change going forward -- functional tests that a claim can be created, routed, approved or denied correctly, plus access-control tests that specifically try to read one partner's claim as a different partner's logged-in test user and confirm that fails. That suite catches regressions fast and runs unattended. The second tier is a pre-launch User Acceptance Testing phase: a small number of real partner companies -- not synthetic test accounts -- actually using the finished portal (and, by the time it exists, the API) against real-looking claims before the other roughly 195 partners get access. ATF is planned to run continuously through the build; the UAT window is planned as a scheduled, time-boxed phase that sits right before go-live, gated the same deliberate way Zara's security review was named as a real gate back in lesson 1 -- not a step anyone gets to skip under launch pressure.

lessons.explainProfessional:
Building starts with the application shell, not the table, because the table has to live inside a scope that already exists. In Studio, Dmitri creates a new application with Name "Partner Warranty Claims" -- Studio derives the scope `x_brind_claims` from that name automatically -- a short description referencing Brindlewood's warranty-claim intake problem, and version 1.0.0. Creating the application registers it in `sys_app` and switches the active development session into the `x_brind_claims` scope, which matters because every table, field, and script built from this point forward in this lesson's work lands inside that scope by default, exactly the isolation decided on back in lesson 4.

The table itself gets created next, as an Application File of type Table, with label "Warranty Claim." Studio derives the table name `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` from the scope prefix and the label. Dmitri leaves "Extends table" blank rather than extending Task -- a deliberate choice, because Task carries its own default state model and assignment semantics that don't match the five specific states (New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed) this table needs to own outright, and inheriting Task's defaults here would mean fighting them later rather than designing cleanly now. Studio's default auto-number display field is kept, with the prefix set to `WTC`, so every claim gets a human-readable identifier like `WTC0001000` the moment it's created, independent of whatever's eventually built on top of the raw record.

With the table created, Dmitri adds the seven fields designed three lessons ago, one at a time, through the table's field list: `partner_company` as a Reference field pointing at the Company [`core_company`] table -- the exact relationship the data-model lesson settled on, reusing Brindlewood's existing partner identity rather than inventing a new one; `equipment_serial` as a plain String field; `issue_description` and `resolution_notes` both as multi-line text fields, sized generously enough that a real description or resolution note won't get truncated; `state` as a Choice field with five values entered in order -- New, In Review, Approved, Denied, Closed -- with New set as the field's default value so every new record starts in a known, consistent state before anything else touches it; `labor_hours` as a Decimal field; and `parts_cost` as a Currency field, so it carries proper currency formatting rather than behaving like a bare number.

Dmitri finishes by creating a simple Application Menu and a single module pointing at the table's default list view, so that an internal user with the right role can navigate to Warranty Claims from the application navigator at all -- without that module, there's no way for anyone, Dmitri included, to even open the table through the UI to confirm it looks right. He does not create any ACL record, any business rule, any Flow, or any Scripted REST resource in this lesson. At this point, any user holding a role with default platform access to custom tables can open any claim record and see any partner's data -- that gap is real, it's expected at this stage of the build, and it's exactly what the next lesson's ACL exists to close. Confirming the table structure against the lesson-5 design document with Zara Ahmed, before any security or automation work begins, is the last thing Dmitri does before moving on.

lessons.title: Building the Row-Level ACL for Partner Isolation
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski builds the real row-level read ACL on x_brind_claims_warranty_claim -- a Script Include that resolves the logged-in user's partner company and compares it to the claim's partner_company field -- correctly enforcing REQ-3 across every native UI surface: list views, form views, and the portal.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
REQ-3 has been sitting in a requirements document since lesson 2: a partner must never see another partner's claims, through any access path. Right now that's still only a written promise. The `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` table exists, with `partner_company`, `equipment_serial`, `issue_description`, `state`, `labor_hours`, `parts_cost`, and `resolution_notes` -- but with no access control configured yet, any logged-in user who can reach the table can read every row in it, regardless of whose claim it is.

This lesson gives Dmitri Kowalski the piece that actually closes that gap for the platform's native UI: a real, row-level read ACL on `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`. The mechanism has two parts. First, a Script Include, `PartnerClaimUtils`, that resolves the logged-in user's own partner company -- the company recorded on their `sys_user` record -- into something comparable. Second, the ACL's own condition script, which calls that Script Include and compares the result against `current.partner_company` on the record being read, granting access only on a match (or to an internal admin or claims-reviewer role).

This is the one lesson in this series where nothing is wrong. Dmitri builds this correctly, tests it against two real partner logins side by side, and it holds up -- because this ACL is exactly what protects every native ServiceNow surface: list views, form views, and, in the next lesson, the partner portal itself.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a filing cabinet with one drawer per client, but no locks on any of the drawers yet -- anyone who can walk up to the cabinet can open any drawer. That's the claims table right now: the data exists, but nothing stops one partner from seeing another partner's folder.

Dmitri's job in this video is to put a real lock on every drawer. He builds a little helper that looks up whose folder you're even allowed to open -- it checks your own badge (your user account) to see which company you work for. Then he builds the actual lock: before the cabinet lets anyone look inside a folder, it checks the name on the folder against the name on your badge. No match, no drawer opens for you. He tests it by badging in as two different people from two different companies, side by side, and each one really can only open their own folders.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The mechanism here is the standard ServiceNow pattern for row-level security on a custom table: a Script Include encapsulates the identity-resolution logic, and the table's ACL -- specifically the read-operation ACL on `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim` -- calls into it from its condition script rather than inlining the logic directly on the ACL record. Keeping the resolution logic in a Script Include matters for more than tidiness: the exact same `PartnerClaimUtils.canUserAccessClaim()` call can be reused anywhere else in the `x_brind_claims` scope that needs the identical check, without re-deriving it.

Identity resolution itself leans on something Brindlewood already has: every `sys_user` record carries a `company` reference field, populated for partner accounts during onboarding, pointing at the same `core_company` table that `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim.partner_company` also references. `PartnerClaimUtils.getCurrentUserPartnerCompany()` reads `gs.getUserID()`, looks up that user's `sys_user.company` value, and returns it (or `null` for an account with no company set -- an internal employee, by design, rather than a partner). `canUserAccessClaim()` takes the claim's `partner_company` value and does a direct sys_id comparison against that resolved company.

The ACL's condition script adds one deliberate carve-out before the comparison ever runs: `gs.hasRole('admin')` or a dedicated `x_brind_claims.claims_reviewer` role short-circuits to `true`, so Brindlewood's own internal reviewers -- who legitimately need to see claims across many partners -- aren't blocked by a check designed for partner-to-partner isolation. That carve-out is scoped narrowly to roles, not to any broader condition, so it doesn't weaken what REQ-3 actually requires between partners.

What makes this lesson's ACL correct, and what the rest of this series eventually contrasts it against, is where the enforcement actually lives: on the `GlideRecord` query engine itself, for any code path that runs through it under the logged-in user's own session. Every native UI surface -- a list view, a form, a related list, the Service Portal widgets built in the next lesson -- queries this table through exactly that path, so this one ACL protects all of them simultaneously, without needing to be re-implemented per surface.

Verified against two real partner logins in both directions plus an internal reviewer account; all native UI surfaces are protected by this single mechanism.

lessons.title: Building the Partner Self-Service Portal UI
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski builds the partner-facing self-service portal -- a claims-list widget and a claim-submission widget -- that correctly shows each partner only their own claims, by deliberately relying on the row-level ACL from the last lesson rather than re-filtering by hand.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the row-level ACL in place, partners still have no actual screen to use. This lesson gives Dmitri Kowalski the partner-facing half of REQ-1: a self-service portal experience, built as two Service Portal widgets, where a partner can see their own warranty claims and submit a new one.

The first widget, "My Warranty Claims," lists every claim belonging to the logged-in partner: claim number, equipment serial, issue description, status, and the labor hours and parts cost once a reviewer has logged them. The second, "Submit a Warranty Claim," is a simple form a partner's technician fills out after a repair -- equipment serial, issue description, labor hours, parts cost -- which creates a new record in `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`.

The detail that matters most in this lesson is what the claims-list widget's server script does *not* do: it doesn't add a query filter for the logged-in partner's own company. It queries the table plainly and trusts the ACL built in the last lesson to do the actual restricting, because that's exactly how a Service Portal widget's GlideRecord query behaves -- it runs in the logged-in user's own session, so the same ACL that protects a list view protects this widget automatically. Dmitri proves it by logging in as two different partners side by side.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a shared library kiosk where, the moment you scan your own card, the screen only ever shows books checked out under your name -- not because the kiosk's software specifically wrote "only show this person's books," but because the whole kiosk is wired to the same library card system that already knows whose books are whose, everywhere in the building.

That's how Dmitri builds the partner portal. The screen that lists "my claims" doesn't have any special code saying "only show claims for this company" -- it just asks for claims the normal way, and the same lock from the last video (the one checking your badge against the folder) quietly does the filtering for it, automatically, the exact same way it would for any other screen in the building. He checks this really works by logging in as two different repair companies, one after another, and each one only ever sees their own.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The claims-list widget's server script is a standard Service Portal pattern: an unfiltered `GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim')` query, ordered by creation date, pushed into the widget's `data` object for the client script and HTML template to render. No `addQuery('partner_company', ...)` call appears anywhere in it, and that omission is deliberate, not an oversight -- Service Portal widget server scripts execute within the rendering request's own authenticated session, which means the `GlideRecord` query engine enforces the exact same ACL stack it enforces for a list view or a form, including the read ACL and Script Include built in the previous lesson. Filtering by hand in the widget would be redundant at best, and at worst would create a second, independently-maintained copy of REQ-3's logic that could quietly drift out of sync with the ACL over time.

The submission widget is a straightforward Service Portal form backed by a server script that performs an `insert` against `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`, setting `partner_company` from the submitting user's own resolved company (via the same `PartnerClaimUtils.getCurrentUserPartnerCompany()` call) rather than trusting any client-submitted value for that field -- the create path gets the same discipline about identity the read path does, even though REQ-3 is framed around reads.

Validation for this lesson is specifically a cross-session comparison, not a single-user smoke test: Dmitri opens two authenticated portal sessions as two different real partner accounts and confirms each one's claims list renders only that partner's own records, with the reviewer-facing fields (labor hours, parts cost, resolution notes) visible once populated. Nothing about this widget introduces a second code path around the ACL -- it's the same GlideRecord-through-ACL mechanism the last lesson already proved correct, exercised now through a UI a partner will actually use.

## Step 1 -- Confirm the portal should lean on the ACL, not re-check it ``` DMITRI: The claims-list widget could filter by partner_company itself, or it could just query the table plainly and let last lesson's ACL do the work. A widget that filters by hand is a widget that can get the filter wrong later without anyone noticing, because it looks like it's working. Let the ACL be the one source of truth. ``` ## Step 2 -- Build the claims-list widget's server script ```javascript (function() { data.claims = []; var gr = new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim'); gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on'); gr.query(); while (gr.next()) { data.claims.push({ number: gr.getValue('number'), equipment_serial: gr.getValue('equipment_serial'), issue_description: gr.getValue('issue_description'), state: gr.getDisplayValue('state'), labor_hours: gr.getValue('labor_hours'), parts_cost: gr.getValue('parts_cost'), resolution_notes: gr.getValue('resolution_notes') }); } })(); ``` No `partner_company` query anywhere -- the ACL restricts the rows `gr.next()` can ever reach. ## Step 3 -- Build the claim-submission widget's server script ```javascript (function() { if (input && input.submit) { var gr = new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim'); gr.initialize(); gr.setValue('partner_company', new x_brind_claims.PartnerClaimUtils() .getCurrentUserPartnerCompany()); gr.setValue('equipment_serial', input.equipment_serial); gr.setValue('issue_description', input.issue_description); gr.setValue('labor_hours', input.labor_hours); gr.setValue('parts_cost', input.parts_cost); gr.insert(); data.submitted = true; } })(); ``` `partner_company` comes from the submitter's own resolved company -- never from the form itself. ## Step 4 -- Build the HTML templates The list widget's template is a simple table bound to `data.claims`: ```html
