lessons.title: Building the Flow Designer Automation for Claim Routing
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski builds a Flow Designer flow that triggers on a new Warranty Claim record, looks up the right internal reviewer based on the equipment's product line, assigns and notifies them, and moves the claim into an Under Review state.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Partners can now submit claims and see their own status, but once a claim lands in `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`, nothing happens to it -- it just sits there until someone on Natalie Fairweather's team happens to notice it. This lesson gives Dmitri Kowalski the piece that closes that gap: a Flow Designer flow that triggers the moment a new Warranty Claim record is created, figures out which internal reviewer should actually look at it, assigns it to them, and notifies them -- the same kind of automated routing a shared inbox could never provide.

Brindlewood's claims naturally sort by product line, and the equipment serial number already encodes that: every serial starts with a two-letter product-line code (`HY` for hydraulic systems, `CN` for conveyor systems, and so on). Dmitri adds a small reference table, `x_brind_claims_product_line`, mapping each code to the internal group responsible for reviewing claims on that product line, and the flow looks up the right group from the new claim's `equipment_serial` prefix.

Once the flow finds a match, it assigns the claim, moves its `state` to "Under Review," and sends the assigned group a notification with a direct link to the claim. If no product-line code matches, it falls back to Natalie's general review group rather than silently stalling. There's no bug here -- this is straightforward, correctly-working automation, verified end to end with a handful of real test claims.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a hospital where, the instant a new patient chart gets created, it has to land on the desk of the right specialist automatically -- not sit in a general inbox until someone happens to glance at it. The hospital already writes a short code on every chart saying what kind of case it is, so a simple rule can read that code and route the chart to the right desk instantly, then ping that specialist so they know it's waiting.

That's what Dmitri builds here. Every piece of equipment's serial number already starts with a little code saying what kind of equipment it is -- hydraulic, conveyor, and so on. The moment a partner submits a new claim, a flow reads that code, looks up which internal team handles that kind of equipment, assigns the claim to them, and sends them a message saying "this is waiting on you." If the code doesn't match anything the flow recognizes, it still doesn't just disappear -- it goes to a general team instead of getting lost.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The flow's trigger is a standard Record Created trigger scoped to `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`, firing synchronously enough that routing happens within moments of a partner's submission rather than on some batch delay. The first real action is a Look Up Record step against the new `x_brind_claims_product_line` table, matching on a substring of the triggering record's `equipment_serial` (its first two characters) against that table's `serial_prefix` field -- a small, explicit mapping table rather than a hardcoded if/else chain in the flow itself, which keeps adding a new product line a data change rather than a flow redesign.

A Flow Designer decision branches on whether that lookup found a match. On a match, an Update Record action sets the triggering claim's `assigned_to` field (or, depending on how Brindlewood wants ownership modeled, assigns to the looked-up group directly) and moves `state` to `Under Review`, followed by a Notification action addressed to that reviewer group with the claim number, equipment serial, and issue description inlined, plus a direct link back to the record. On no match, the same Update Record and Notification actions run against Natalie's general review group instead, so an unmapped product-line code degrades to a safe, human-reviewed fallback rather than leaving the claim unassigned and unnoticed.

Dmitri validates this with a handful of test claims spanning known product-line codes, an unrecognized code, and a rapid back-to-back submission to confirm the flow doesn't miss or double-process any record -- each lands correctly assigned, correctly notified, and correctly stated, with the flow's own execution log showing a clean run for every case.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the routing rule with Natalie

```
DMITRI:    Routing claims to the right reviewer -- what actually
           determines who should look at a given claim?

NATALIE:   Product line, mostly. Hydraulic claims go to one team,
           conveyor systems go to another, and so on. The equipment
           serial already tells you which one -- the first two
           letters are a product code every tech already recognizes.

DMITRI:    Good -- that's something I can look up automatically
           instead of asking partners to pick a category by hand.
```

## Step 2 -- Build the product-line lookup table

A small table, `x_brind_claims_product_line`, with `serial_prefix` (e.g. `HY`, `CN`), `product_line_name`, and `reviewer_group` (reference to `sys_user_group`). Dmitri and Natalie populate it together with Brindlewood's real product lines and the teams that already own them.

## Step 3 -- Build the flow trigger

In Flow Designer: trigger type **Record Created**, table `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`, condition left open (every new claim needs routing).

## Step 4 -- Look up the reviewer group

Add a **Look Up Record** action against `x_brind_claims_product_line`, matching `serial_prefix` to the first two characters of the trigger record's `equipment_serial`:

```
Look Up Record
  Table: x_brind_claims_product_line
  Condition: serial_prefix = {{trigger.equipment_serial}}.substring(0, 2)
```

## Step 5 -- Branch, assign, and notify

A **Decision** step checks whether the lookup returned a record. On match:

```
Update Record (trigger.current)
  assigned_to = {{lookup.reviewer_group}}
  state = Under Review

Notification
  Recipient: {{lookup.reviewer_group}}
  Message: New warranty claim {{trigger.number}} ({{trigger.equipment_serial}})
           assigned for review: {{trigger.issue_description}}
```

On no match, the same two actions run against Natalie's general review group instead, so nothing goes unassigned.

## Step 6 -- Test end to end and confirm

```
DMITRI:    Submitted a test claim with a hydraulic-line serial --
           it's assigned to the Hydraulics review team within
           seconds, state moved to Under Review, and the group got
           the notification.

DMITRI:    Tried an unrecognized serial prefix next -- it fell back
           to the general review group exactly as designed, nothing
           got stuck unassigned.

DMITRI:    Submitted two claims back to back, different product
           lines, to make sure the flow doesn't cross-assign or
           drop one of them under load.
```

## Step 7 -- Check the flow's own execution log

Dmitri pulls up the flow's execution history for each test claim and confirms every run shows a clean "Completed" status, with the lookup, update, and notification steps each logging the exact values they acted on -- not just that the flow finished, but that it finished having touched the record it was supposed to touch.

```
DMITRI:    Execution log for the hydraulic test claim shows the
           lookup matching HY to the Hydraulics group, the update
           setting assigned_to and state, and the notification
           firing to that exact group -- no silent partial runs.

NATALIE:   That's a real improvement over watching a shared inbox.
           Claims land on the right desk the moment they're
           submitted, and now I can actually see proof of that in
           the flow's own history if anyone ever asks.
```

With routing live and verified, the next lesson gives partners' own field-service software a way to reach Brindlewood directly, without a person at a keyboard at all.

Verified against known product-line codes, an unrecognized code, and rapid-fire submissions.

lessons.title: Building the Scripted REST API for Partner Integrations
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski builds a Scripted REST API -- GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims -- so partners' own field-service software can query claims programmatically. The GET handler uses plain GlideRecord filtered by a partner_company request parameter; the team tests it by calling it as Partner A and confirming Partner A's own claims come back correctly.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The portal satisfies REQ-1, but REQ-2 is still open: partners' own field-service software -- the scheduling tools and mobile apps their technicians already use in the field -- has no way to reach Brindlewood at all. A partner's backend can't click through a web form. This lesson gives Dmitri Kowalski the piece that closes that gap: a Scripted REST API, in the `x_brind_claims` scope, that lets a partner's own system create and query warranty claims directly.

This lesson builds the read side: a resource at `/api/x_brind_claims/claims`, handling `GET` requests, so a partner's software can pull claim status without a person involved. A partner authenticates the same way any Brindlewood integration partner does -- credentials Brindlewood issues them for this API -- and passes a `partner_company` query parameter identifying whose claims to return, along with optional filters for `state` and `equipment_serial`.

The handler itself is a clean, ordinary implementation: a plain `GlideRecord` query against `x_brind_claims_warranty_claim`, filtered on the request parameters, looped over to build the JSON response. Dmitri and the team test it the way you'd expect a new integration endpoint to get tested before shipping: authenticate as a real partner, Driscoll Mechanical Services, pass Driscoll's own `partner_company` value, and confirm Driscoll's own claims come back correctly formatted. They do, every time. The API is ready for partners' field-service software to start integrating against.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a vending machine that, up until now, only had a coin slot a person could physically walk up to and use. Some of Brindlewood's partners don't have a person checking a website every day -- they have their own computer systems that want to ask "what's the status of my claims?" automatically, the same way a delivery app checks on an order without a person opening a browser.

Dmitri builds a new kind of door into the claims data: one a computer program can knock on directly, using a login Brindlewood hands out and a simple question -- "show me the claims for this company." The team tests it the obvious way: they knock on that door pretending to be one real partner, ask for that partner's own claims, and the right claims come back, correctly, every time they try it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the shape of the API with Natalie

```
DMITRI:    For partners' own software to pull claim status, I'm
           building a GET endpoint: pass your partner_company, get
           back your claims. Optionally filter by state or equipment
           serial too.

NATALIE:   That matches what partners have been asking for -- their
           own system checking in automatically instead of someone
           refreshing a web page.
```

## Step 2 -- Create the Scripted REST API resource

In **System Web Services > Scripted REST APIs**, Dmitri creates a new API in the `x_brind_claims` scope, base path `/api/x_brind_claims`, and adds a resource:

```
Resource name: Claims
HTTP method:   GET
Relative path: /claims
```

## Step 3 -- Write the GET handler

```javascript
(function process(/*RESTAPIRequest*/ request, /*RESTAPIResponse*/ response) {
    var partnerCompany = request.queryParams.partner_company;
    if (!partnerCompany) {
        response.setStatus(400);
        response.setBody({ error: 'partner_company is required' });
        return;
    }

    var gr = new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim');
    gr.addQuery('partner_company', partnerCompany);

    if (request.queryParams.state) {
        gr.addQuery('state', request.queryParams.state);
    }
    if (request.queryParams.equipment_serial) {
        gr.addQuery('equipment_serial', request.queryParams.equipment_serial);
    }

    gr.query();

    var claims = [];
    while (gr.next()) {
        claims.push({
            sys_id: gr.getUniqueValue(),
            number: gr.getValue('number'),
            partner_company: gr.getDisplayValue('partner_company'),
            equipment_serial: gr.getValue('equipment_serial'),
            issue_description: gr.getValue('issue_description'),
            state: gr.getDisplayValue('state'),
            labor_hours: gr.getValue('labor_hours'),
            parts_cost: gr.getValue('parts_cost'),
            resolution_notes: gr.getValue('resolution_notes')
        });
    }

    response.setStatus(200);
    response.setBody({ result: claims });
})(request, response);
```

## Step 4 -- Issue integration credentials to a real partner

Dmitri sets up a dedicated set of API credentials for Driscoll Mechanical Services, the same way Brindlewood issues credentials to any integration partner, and shares the base URL and resource path with their integration contact.

## Step 5 -- Test as Driscoll, requesting Driscoll's own claims

```bash
curl -u driscoll_api_user:********* \
  "https://brindlewood.service-now.com/api/x_brind_claims/claims?partner_company=<driscoll_company_sys_id>"
```

```
DMITRI:    Called it authenticated as Driscoll, passing Driscoll's
           own partner_company value -- got back exactly Driscoll's
           claims, correctly formatted. Tried it again with a state
           filter and an equipment_serial filter -- both narrowed the
           results correctly.

NATALIE:   And that's using the real credentials we'd actually hand a
           partner?

DMITRI:    Yes -- this is exactly what Driscoll's own system would
           call once we give them these credentials.
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm the required-parameter and error handling

```
DMITRI:    Calling the endpoint with no partner_company at all
           returns a clean 400 and an error message, rather than
           quietly querying the whole table or throwing an
           unhandled script error. Calling it with a partner_company
           value that matches nothing returns a 200 with an empty
           result array, which is the correct response for "this
           partner exists but has no claims yet."
```

## Step 7 -- Write a short integration note for partners

Dmitri writes a brief reference for partners' own developers, documenting the endpoint, its required and optional parameters, and a sample response, so Driscoll's team -- and the next partner who wants to integrate -- isn't reverse-engineering the API from trial and error:

```
GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims
  Required:  partner_company (your Brindlewood partner company id)
  Optional:  state, equipment_serial
  Returns:   { "result": [ { number, equipment_serial,
              issue_description, state, labor_hours, parts_cost,
              resolution_notes }, ... ] }
```

## Step 8 -- Confirm and ship it

```
DMITRI:    The GET endpoint is live, documented, handles the missing-
           parameter case cleanly, and returns correct data for a
           real partner's own claims every time we've called it.
           REQ-2's query side is done.

NATALIE:   Great -- let's get this in front of a couple more partners
           who've been asking for it.
```

With the API live, Brindlewood now has every piece of V1 the scope document named: the application, the ACL, the portal, the automation, and the API. The next lesson puts the whole thing through a full rehearsal together.

Verified by authenticating as Driscoll Mechanical Services and confirming Driscoll's own partner_company value returns Driscoll's own claims correctly, including with the optional filters applied.

lessons.title: Writing Automated Test Framework Coverage for the Claims Workflow
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski builds a real ATF suite for x_brind_claims covering partner claim creation, Flow Designer routing, and the portal's partner-only visibility -- solid, real coverage of every path a user reaches through the UI.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The portal, the Flow Designer automation, and the Scripted REST API for x_brind_claims are all built. Before any of it goes anywhere near production, Dmitri Kowalski wants a safety net that doesn't depend on a human remembering to click through every screen by hand after the next deploy. That safety net is ServiceNow's Automated Test Framework (ATF), and this lesson is Dmitri building three real, reasonably thorough tests against the warranty claims workflow.

The first test proves a partner can actually create a claim the way the portal is designed to let them: impersonate a real partner test user, open the warranty claim form through the portal widget, fill in the real fields -- equipment_serial, issue_description -- and submit, then assert the record landed in x_brind_claims_warranty_claim with partner_company populated correctly from the logged-in user's own company. The second test proves the Flow Designer automation that was built to route a new claim actually fires and does its job: a new x_brind_claims_warranty_claim record gets created, the test waits for the flow to run, and then asserts the record's state and assignment group ended up where the flow is supposed to put them. The third test proves the one thing Natalie Fairweather has been most worried about since the very first requirements conversation: that a partner logging into the portal sees only their own company's claims, never another partner's -- seeded with claims from two different partner companies, impersonated as one of them, and asserted that only that partner's claims show up in the portal's list.

Three tests, each exercising a real path a real user takes through the system Dmitri's team actually built: create a claim, have it route correctly, see only your own data. All three pass clean, and Dmitri adds them to a permanent ATF test suite that will run automatically on every future change to this scoped app.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about the checks a car gets before it leaves the factory: does the key start the engine, do the turn signals work when you flip the lever, does the dashboard show your own fuel gauge and not some other car's. Nobody drives the car through every possible pothole in the world first -- they check that the normal, everyday things a normal driver does all work correctly, every single time, automatically, without a person having to climb in and try it themselves after every tweak to the assembly line.

That's what Dmitri builds here. He writes three automatic checks for the warranty claims system: can a partner actually submit a claim, does it get routed to the right place afterward, and does a partner see only their own claims and not someone else's when they log in. Each one gets tested by literally pretending to be a partner user and clicking through the real screens, except a computer does the clicking instead of a person, and it does it the exact same way every single time from now on, automatically, whenever anyone changes anything about this system.
lessons.explainProfessional:
ATF earns its place in a scoped-app rollout precisely because manual regression testing doesn't scale past the second or third release -- a human QA pass against three workflows might get run faithfully before go-live and then quietly skipped three sprints later when a deadline is tight, and that's exactly when a regression slips through. Each of these three tests is built from standard ATF step types: Impersonate User to assume a real partner test account's session, Open New Record and Set Field Values to drive the portal's own form rather than inserting data server-side (which would prove nothing about the portal UI itself), and a Server-Side step purely for test-data scaffolding where the scenario calls for pre-existing records rather than ones the test itself creates.

The Flow Designer test is worth calling out specifically, because testing an asynchronous flow is a different problem than testing a synchronous form submission: the test has to account for the flow actually completing before it asserts against the record's state, which is why it uses a Wait for Condition step rather than asserting immediately after the triggering insert. Get that ordering wrong and the test is flaky -- passing or failing depending on how fast the flow engine happens to run that day -- which is worse than no test at all, because a flaky test trains the team to ignore its failures.

What this suite validates, precisely, is every path a user reaches by going through the product the way it was designed to be used: the portal form, the flow it triggers, and the portal's own list view. That's real, substantial coverage, and it's the coverage most teams stop at before go-live.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Seed two partner companies and their test users

Before writing any test, Dmitri needs real test data spanning more than one partner company, so the portal-visibility test has something to actually distinguish. He creates two partner company test users under Owen Castellano's existing partner account structure:

```
Test user: priya.test.driscoll  -- company: Driscoll Mechanical Services
Test user: marcus.test.castlerock -- company: Castle Rock Tooling
```

Each is a real sys_user record with the company field set, the same field the table's ACL checks against.

## Step 2 -- ATF Test: Partner Creates a Warranty Claim

```
Test: ATF - Partner Creates Warranty Claim
  1. Impersonate User -- priya.test.driscoll
  2. Open New Record -- Warranty Claim (portal widget)
  3. Set Field Values -- equipment_serial: "PRS-4471"
                          issue_description: "Hydraulic press leaking at seal"
  4. Submit Form
  5. Field Value Assertion -- partner_company equals "Driscoll Mechanical Services"
  6. Field Value Assertion -- state equals "New"
```

The assertion on partner_company matters as much as the submit succeeding -- it confirms the form (or a business rule behind it) is stamping the logged-in user's own company onto the record, not leaving it blank or editable.

## Step 3 -- ATF Test: Flow Designer Routes the New Claim

```
Test: ATF - New Claim Routes via Flow Designer
  1. Server-Side Step -- insert x_brind_claims_warranty_claim record
     (equipment_serial: "PRS-4471", partner_company: Driscoll Mechanical Services)
  2. Wait for Condition -- record's state changes from "New"
     (timeout: 30 seconds)
  3. Field Value Assertion -- state equals "Assigned"
  4. Field Value Assertion -- assignment_group equals "Warranty Claims Review"
```

The Wait for Condition step is deliberate -- the flow runs asynchronously, so asserting immediately after the insert would make this test flaky.

## Step 4 -- ATF Test: Portal Shows a Partner Only Their Own Claims

```
Test: ATF - Portal Visibility is Partner-Scoped
  1. Server-Side Step -- seed one claim for Driscoll Mechanical Services,
     one claim for Castle Rock Tooling
  2. Impersonate User -- priya.test.driscoll
  3. Open Portal Page -- My Warranty Claims
  4. Related List Content Assertion -- list contains Driscoll's claim sys_id
  5. Related List Content Assertion -- list does NOT contain
     Castle Rock Tooling's claim sys_id
```

This is the test that actually exercises the row-level ACL from the portal side, end to end, rather than trusting the ACL configuration by itself.

## Step 5 -- Assemble the ATF Test Suite

Dmitri groups all three into a single suite so they run together on every future change:

```
ATF Test Suite: Warranty Claims - Pre-Launch Regression
  - ATF - Partner Creates Warranty Claim
  - ATF - New Claim Routes via Flow Designer
  - ATF - Portal Visibility is Partner-Scoped
```

## Step 6 -- Run the suite and review results

```
TEST SUITE RUN -- Warranty Claims - Pre-Launch Regression
  ATF - Partner Creates Warranty Claim ........ PASS
  ATF - New Claim Routes via Flow Designer ..... PASS
  ATF - Portal Visibility is Partner-Scoped ..... PASS
  3 of 3 passing
```

Three for three, clean. Dmitri schedules the suite to run nightly against the sub-production instance, so any future change to the portal, the flow, or the ACL gets caught automatically instead of waiting for someone to notice by hand.

All three pass; suite is scheduled to run nightly.

These run automatically from now on, so we'll catch any accidental breakage before it reaches partners.

These checks run on their own going forward, which protects us from accidental regressions as we keep improving the system after launch.

lessons.title: Running the Pre-Launch UAT With Real Partner Accounts
lessons.summary: Natalie Fairweather runs UAT with real accounts from Driscoll Mechanical Services, Castle Rock Tooling, and Vantage Precision Group -- partners submit test claims, confirm they see only their own through the portal, and Holly Vance confirms her own API integration works. Clean sign-off, no trouble found.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
ATF proves the system behaves correctly in the lab. Natalie Fairweather wants proof it behaves correctly for the actual people who will use it, which means UAT with real accounts from real partner companies, not test users Dmitri invented himself. Owen Castellano provisions real portal logins tied to three actual Brindlewood partners -- Driscoll Mechanical Services, Castle Rock Tooling, and Vantage Precision Group -- each pointed at that company's own partner_company value on the account record.

Each partner's contact logs into the live portal, submits a real test warranty claim the way they would for an actual piece of equipment, and confirms in their own browser, under their own login, that the claim shows up in their list -- and that nothing from either of the other two companies shows up alongside it. Holly Vance, Driscoll's IT contact, goes a step further on Driscoll's side: her team has been building their own internal integration against the Scripted REST API, and this is their chance to test it against the real, live endpoint for the first time using Driscoll's own API credentials. She queries for Driscoll's own claims and confirms the right data comes back, formatted the way her integration expects.

Every partner confirms the portal experience works exactly as intended. Priya confirms her integration pulls Driscoll's own claims correctly. Natalie collects the feedback -- a couple of small, cosmetic requests about field labels, nothing structural -- and closes out UAT with a clean sign-off. The team feels good about the go-live date.
lessons.explainSimple:
Before a restaurant opens to the public, it doesn't just trust the kitchen staff's own taste tests -- it invites a few real, ordinary customers in for a quiet trial dinner, lets them order for real, and watches whether the whole experience actually works for someone who isn't already an expert on the menu.

That's UAT. Instead of Dmitri's own test accounts, three real partner companies get real logins and submit real test requests through the actual website, the same way they'll do it after launch. Each one checks their own receipt and confirms they only see their own order, never someone else's. One of the partners, Driscoll, also has their own technical team plug their internal systems into Brindlewood's data feed and confirm they're getting their own information back correctly. Everyone comes away happy, and the team feels ready to open the doors for real.
lessons.explainProfessional:
UAT with real partner accounts validates something ATF, by design, can't: whether the system behaves correctly for people who didn't build it, using credentials and company associations that were provisioned the normal way rather than scaffolded by a test script. That distinction matters more here than it might elsewhere, because the portal's row-level ACL depends entirely on each user's company association being correct in the platform's own user-management data -- a test user Dmitri creates and a real partner contact Owen provisions through the normal process are, in principle, exercising the identical ACL check, but only the second one proves the real provisioning path produces a user record the ACL actually evaluates the way everyone expects.

It's worth being precise about what Holly Vance's API test does and doesn't prove, because the distinction matters a great deal very soon. She authenticates with Driscoll's own credentials, queries for Driscoll's own data, and gets back exactly what she expects -- a completely reasonable integration test for a partner confirming their own pipeline works. That is a meaningfully different test than one partner's credentials attempting to retrieve another partner's data through that same endpoint; UAT is designed to confirm the system does what it's supposed to do for the users it's built for, which is exactly what it confirms here, cleanly, for all three partners and for Holly's integration. Whether that same endpoint also refuses to do what it isn't supposed to do is a different question, deliberately out of UAT's scope -- that's what a dedicated security review exists to check.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Owen provisions real portal accounts for three partner companies

Owen Castellano sets up live portal logins tied to real partner company records, not test-only accounts:

```
Driscoll Mechanical Services  -- contact: Holly Vance (IT contact)
Castle Rock Tooling       -- contact: Tom Reilly (Service Coordinator)
Vantage Precision Group   -- contact: Elena Ruiz (Operations Lead)
```

Each account's company field is set to that partner's actual partner_company value, the same field the ACL and portal rely on.

## Step 2 -- Each partner submits a real test claim through the portal

Tom Reilly logs into the portal himself and submits:

```
Equipment serial: CRT-8820
Issue description: Conveyor motor overheating under load
```

Elena Ruiz and Holly Vance each do the same for a piece of Vantage and Driscoll equipment respectively. Three real claims, submitted by three real people, through the real, live portal -- not seeded by a script.

## Step 3 -- Each partner confirms they see only their own claim

Each contact opens their own "My Warranty Claims" list in the portal and confirms:

```
Tom Reilly (Castle Rock Tooling)    -- sees CRT-8820, nothing else
Elena Ruiz (Vantage Precision Group) -- sees her own claim, nothing else
Holly Vance (Driscoll Mechanical Services) -- sees her own claim, nothing else
```

No partner can see either of the other two companies' claims anywhere in the portal. The row-level ACL, exercised by real accounts through the real UI, holds. Dmitri also has each contact try editing a field on their own claim and confirms the update saves correctly, and tries scrolling and refreshing the list a few times to rule out any caching artifact that might briefly surface a stale cross-partner result -- nothing does.

## Step 4 -- Holly Vance tests Driscoll's own API integration

Holly's team has their own internal system calling the Scripted REST API. She runs it against the live endpoint using Driscoll's own API credentials:

```
GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims?partner_company=<Driscoll_Mechanical_Services_sys_id>
Authorization: Basic <Driscoll API credentials>
```

```json
{
  "result": [
    { "sys_id": "a93f...", "partner_company": "Driscoll Mechanical Services",
      "equipment_serial": "PRS-4471", "state": "New" }
  ]
}
```

Exactly Driscoll's own claim comes back, formatted the way her integration expects. She confirms the integration works and doesn't test any query beyond her own company's data -- that's not what this test was for.

## Step 5 -- Collect feedback

```
UAT FEEDBACK LOG
  Tom Reilly: "Could the 'Issue Description' label be clearer?" -- cosmetic, logged
  Elena Ruiz: "Confirmation message could be more specific." -- cosmetic, logged
  Holly Vance: "Integration pulled our data correctly, no issues."
```

Nothing structural. All three partners confirm the core experience -- submit a claim, see only your own -- works exactly as intended.

## Step 6 -- Natalie signs off

```
UAT SIGN-OFF -- x_brind_claims, Partner Portal
  Driscoll Mechanical Services:  claim submitted, visibility confirmed -- PASS
  Castle Rock Tooling:       claim submitted, visibility confirmed -- PASS
  Vantage Precision Group:   claim submitted, visibility confirmed -- PASS
  Driscoll API integration:  own-data query confirmed working -- PASS
  Minor UI feedback logged, no blockers.
  Sign-off: Natalie Fairweather -- ready for go-live.
```

Clean UAT, real partners, real accounts. The team feels confident heading toward the launch date.

lessons.title: The Security Review That Found a Cross-Partner Data Leak
lessons.summary: Zara Ahmed's dedicated security review calls the Scripted REST API directly as a Driscoll test user with a broad query and gets back Castle Rock Tooling and Vantage Precision Group's warranty claims too -- the table's ACL is correct, but the API script uses plain GlideRecord and never consults it. Confirmed and reported, not yet fixed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
UAT confirmed the portal works correctly for partners doing exactly what they're supposed to do. That is not the same thing as confirming the system can't be made to do something it isn't supposed to do, and Zara Ahmed, Brindlewood's ServiceNow Technical Architect, treats that distinction as the entire point of the dedicated security review she runs before go-live. She doesn't click through the portal looking for broken buttons. She picks up a REST client, authenticates as a real Driscoll test user, and starts testing the Scripted REST API directly, the way an actual attacker -- or a partner who's simply curious -- would.

She calls the live /api/x_brind_claims/claims endpoint authenticated as Driscoll's own test user, but instead of scoping her query to Driscoll's own data the way Holly Vance's integration did in UAT, she sends a broad query that doesn't filter by partner_company at all. The response comes back with warranty claims belonging to Castle Rock Tooling and Vantage Precision Group mixed in with Driscoll's own -- a real, exploitable cross-partner data leak, and a serious one specifically because Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners frequently compete directly against each other in the same local markets. A claim's issue_description and resolution_notes can describe exactly what's failing on a competitor's equipment and how it got fixed.

Zara doesn't assume the ACL is broken -- she checks it first. The table's access control, built back when the team scoped this project, correctly compares the logged-in user's company against the record's partner_company field, and it correctly blocks exactly this kind of cross-partner access everywhere the portal uses it. So she looks at the one place that isn't the portal: the Scripted REST API's GET handler script itself. It queries x_brind_claims_warranty_claim with a plain GlideRecord. The ACL isn't being bypassed because anyone wrote it wrong. It's being bypassed because this particular script never asks it anything at all. She writes the finding up precisely and reports it to Dmitri Kowalski and Natalie Fairweather immediately. Nothing is fixed yet -- that's the next lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine an office building where every door into every company's private floor requires swiping a badge that only opens your own floor's door -- a really well-built, correctly working security system. Now imagine there's also a mail chute in the basement that delivers packages straight to any floor's mailroom if you just write the floor number on the package, no badge required, because whoever installed the mail chute forgot the badge system existed.

That's exactly what Zara finds. The front door -- the website partners actually log into -- has a badge reader that works perfectly; every partner who's walked through it only ever reaches their own floor. But there's a second way into the same building, a direct data connection meant for computer systems instead of people, and Zara discovers that door has no badge reader on it at all. She proves it by walking straight through it herself, using her own legitimate badge, and finding she can read mail addressed to other companies' floors anyway. She immediately tells Dmitri and Natalie exactly what she found and exactly why it happened. Nobody's fixed the door yet -- that's next.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is worth reading as a template for how a real pre-launch security review differs from functional UAT, and the difference is methodological, not just a matter of trying harder. UAT exercises the system the way an intended user uses it; a security review deliberately exercises the system the way an unintended use case might, and the first place Zara looks is exactly the place UAT didn't cover: a direct API call, authenticated correctly but queried broadly, bypassing the UI entirely. That single methodological choice -- query the endpoint directly with a tool like Postman rather than clicking through the portal -- is what surfaces a defect that a UI-only test pass, however thorough, structurally cannot find.

The diagnosis itself is precise and worth stating carefully, because it's the exact detail lesson 16 depends on. ServiceNow's row-level ACL on x_brind_claims_warranty_claim is correctly written and correctly enforced everywhere the platform's own UI and GlideRecordSecure-aware paths evaluate it. Plain GlideRecord, used in a server-side Scripted REST API script, runs with the script's own elevated execution context and does not automatically evaluate table-level or row-level ACLs the way the native UI does -- it is, by platform design, a security-unaware query object. That means the API script's new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim') call was never wrong in the sense of containing a logic bug; it simply never asked the ACL anything, for every single request it has ever served since the API went live.

It's worth naming precisely what this is not: it is not an ACL misconfiguration, and treating it as one would lead someone to go re-audit the ACL script itself, find nothing wrong, and move on without fixing anything. The vulnerability lives entirely in the choice of query object in one script, independent of how carefully the ACL was written. Confirmed, scoped, and reported to Dmitri and Natalie. The fix is the next lesson, and it has to change the script, not the ACL.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran the Scripted REST API's GET /claims endpoint directly as a Driscoll test user, passing Castle Rock Tooling's partner_company value instead of Driscoll's own, and got back Castle Rock Tooling's claim anyway, including resolution_notes. Confirmed the table's read ACL is correctly written and correctly protects the portal everywhere it's consulted; the API's GET handler uses plain GlideRecord, which never evaluates ACLs at all. Reported to Dmitri and Natalie. Not yet fixed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: During the pre-launch security review, Zara found that our partner API can currently return other partners' claim data when queried directly, bypassing the portal entirely -- which is especially serious since many of our partners compete with each other locally. This is exactly why we built in a dedicated security review before go-live. She's confirmed exactly why it's happening and reported it; the fix starts immediately.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our pre-launch security review caught a serious issue before any partner could be affected by it -- exactly what this review step exists to do. A gap in one integration point could have let a partner see another partner's service data, which matters a great deal given how often our partners compete with each other. No partner data has actually been exposed outside our own testing; this was found and proven safely before launch. We're fixing it now and it will be independently re-verified before we proceed.

lessons.title: Fixing the API With GlideRecordSecure -- and Locking It In
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski swaps plain GlideRecord for GlideRecordSecure in the Scripted REST API's GET handler, re-tests Zara's exact scenario to confirm only a partner's own claims come back now, adds a permanent cross-partner test to the pre-launch checklist and ATF suite, and documents the platform lesson: an ACL only protects the paths that actually consult it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Zara's finding gave Dmitri Kowalski something precise to fix, and like any real fix for a security defect, it isn't one change -- it's four, each closing a different part of the gap.

The direct fix is the smallest possible code change with the largest possible effect: swap new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim') for new GlideRecordSecure('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim') in the GET handler. GlideRecordSecure is a drop-in replacement -- same query methods, same .next(), same .getValue() -- except it automatically enforces every ACL on the table it queries, the same ACL that's been correctly protecting the portal the whole time. The second step is proving it: Dmitri re-runs Zara's exact exploit, the same broad, unfiltered query authenticated as the same Driscoll test user, against the fixed script, and confirms only Driscoll's own claim comes back now -- Castle Rock Tooling's and Vantage Precision Group's claims are gone from the response, not because they were filtered out by a new line of custom logic, but because the existing, already-correct ACL from the very first weeks of this project is finally being asked.

The third step is the one that makes sure this specific class of bug doesn't quietly reappear the next time someone adds an integration point: a permanent entry goes into the pre-launch security checklist, and a new, permanent ATF test gets added to the suite from lesson 13, specifically calling the API as a low-privilege partner user attempting to retrieve another partner's data -- not just confirming the API returns a partner's own data correctly, which is the test that already existed and the test that let this slip through in the first place.

The fourth step isn't a code change at all. Dmitri and Zara write down the underlying platform lesson plainly, for the team and for anyone who touches this scoped app later: in ServiceNow, a server-side script using plain GlideRecord does not automatically inherit ACL enforcement the way the native UI does. GlideRecordSecure, or explicit .canRead() / .canWrite() checks, has to be a deliberate choice an engineer makes every time a new script queries a table with an ACL on it -- never an assumption.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the mail chute with no badge reader, the one that quietly delivered packages to the wrong floor? Here's how it gets fixed, in four separate ways, each one on purpose.

First, the obvious fix: install the exact same badge reader on the mail chute that's already on the front door. It's the same reader, already proven to work correctly -- it just needed to actually be installed on this second entrance too. Second, someone walks through the fixed mail chute exactly the way the problem was first discovered, to prove the badge reader is really there and really working, not just assumed to be.

Third, and this is the part that matters for every future year this building stands: a permanent rule gets written down and a permanent, automatic check gets added -- anytime anyone builds a new door into this building, someone has to specifically try using somebody else's badge on it before it opens to the public, not just confirm your own badge works on your own floor. Fourth, everyone involved writes down, in plain language, the actual lesson: just because a security badge system is correctly installed on one door doesn't mean a brand-new door automatically has it too. Someone has to remember to add it, every single time, on purpose.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The four fixes map cleanly onto four different failure modes, which is exactly why collapsing them into a single line-level patch would have left real risk on the table. The direct fix -- replacing GlideRecord with GlideRecordSecure -- is correct and minimal for this exact script: GlideRecordSecure exposes the identical query API (addEncodedQuery, query, next, getValue, getDisplayValue) so the rest of the handler's logic is untouched, while automatically evaluating the table's ACLs against the requesting user's session for every row returned. This is the right fix for this script, and it's necessary -- but it only closes this one entry point.

That's precisely why re-running Zara's exact exploit against the fixed script matters more than it might look. Confirming only Driscoll's own claim comes back on the identical broad, unfiltered query, authenticated as the identical test user, is the validation step that closes this incident -- proof the ACL is now being consulted, not just confidence that it should be. It also confirms something subtler and important: the fix required zero changes to the ACL itself, because the ACL was never the defect. Changing the ACL to compensate for a script that ignores it would have been exactly the wrong fix, patching the wrong layer.

The third and fourth steps are the ones most teams skip under launch pressure, and they're arguably the ones that matter most over this scoped app's lifetime. A permanent ATF test -- calling the API as a low-privilege partner user and specifically attempting to retrieve another partner's data -- closes the actual coverage gap from lesson 13's test suite, which tested that the API returns a partner's own data correctly but never tested that it refuses another partner's data. Those are not the same test, and a suite that only ever exercises the first one, however faithfully, will never catch a vulnerability that only the second one can surface. Writing the underlying platform lesson down plainly -- that plain GlideRecord does not automatically enforce ACLs the way the native UI does, and that GlideRecordSecure or explicit .canRead()/.canWrite() checks have to be a deliberate choice on every new integration point -- is what prevents this exact class of defect from reappearing the next time someone builds a Script Include, a scheduled job, or another Scripted REST API against a table that has an ACL on it. An ACL that's correctly written only protects the paths that actually consult it; a new integration point has to be deliberately checked against that same security model, never assumed to inherit it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Fixed the Scripted REST API by swapping new GlideRecord() for new GlideRecordSecure() in the GET handler -- a drop-in change that makes the table's existing, already-correct ACL actually get enforced. Re-ran Zara's exact broad-query exploit as the same Driscoll test user; only Driscoll's own claim comes back now. Added a permanent ATF test that calls the API as a low-privilege partner attempting to retrieve another partner's data, and a permanent pre-launch checklist entry requiring that same test pattern for any future Scripted REST API or Script Include against an ACL'd table. Zara re-verified and signed off.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The issue Zara found is fully fixed: we corrected the one line of code causing it, re-tested the exact scenario she used to find it, and -- just as important -- added a permanent automated check and a permanent checklist rule so this specific category of mistake gets caught automatically on any future integration we build, not just during a one-time review. Zara has re-verified and signed off, and we're cleared for go-live.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The issue our security review found before launch has been fully resolved and independently re-verified. We've also put a permanent safeguard in place -- both an automated test and a standing rule for how we build future integrations -- so this exact type of issue gets caught automatically going forward. We're now cleared to proceed toward go-live.

lessons.title: Presenting the Real Results -- and the Security Finding, Honestly
lessons.summary: Dmitri Kowalski and Zara Ahmed present the finished, security-reviewed Partner Warranty Claims application to Natalie Fairweather and Brindlewood leadership -- honest framing of what shipped and full honesty about the cross-partner data-leak vulnerability's discovery and fix, framed as the security review process working exactly as intended.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over sixteen prior lessons, Dmitri Kowalski and the Brindlewood Industrial team built x_brind_claims, the Partner Warranty Claims scoped application, end to end: the Warranty Claim table, a row-level ACL that correctly restricts each partner to their own company's records, a partner self-service portal, Flow Designer automation that routes new claims to the right reviewer, and a Scripted REST API so partners can connect their own systems. A real Automated Test Framework suite passed cleanly, and a pre-launch UAT with real accounts from Driscoll Mechanical Services, Castle Rock Tooling, and Vantage Precision Group confirmed the portal works exactly as intended.

Then Zara Ahmed's dedicated pre-launch security review found something UAT was never designed to find: the Scripted REST API's GET handler filtered strictly by whatever `partner_company` value a caller supplied, using plain GlideRecord, which doesn't automatically enforce the table's correctly-written ACL. An authenticated Driscoll test user who passed Castle Rock Tooling's `partner_company` value instead of their own got Castle Rock's claim back anyway, including commercially sensitive `resolution_notes`. Dmitri fixed it by swapping in GlideRecordSecure, re-verified Zara's exact exploit now returns nothing, and locked the fix in with a permanent ATF test and a standing security-checklist entry.

In this lesson, Dmitri and Zara stand in front of Natalie Fairweather and Brindlewood leadership and present both halves honestly: the real, working application that's ready to go live, and the specific vulnerability that almost shipped with it -- framed not as something to apologize for, but as the security review process catching exactly what it exists to catch, before a single partner's commercially sensitive data was ever actually exposed to a competitor.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a company builds a shared storage facility for about 200 different small businesses, each renting their own locked unit. Every unit has a keycard reader that only opens that business's own door, and it works perfectly, every single time, for every customer who's ever tried it. But there's also a side loading dock meant for delivery trucks instead of people, and when the building's safety inspector tries it herself, she discovers that dock has no keycard reader installed at all -- if you simply write a different unit number on the delivery slip, the dock opens that unit's door for you, no matter whose keycard got you into the building in the first place.

That's almost exactly what happened at Brindlewood Industrial. Dmitri built a website where about 200 partner companies log in and see their own warranty claims, and that website's front door only ever opens to your own claims, tested over and over. But there was also a second way in, a direct data connection meant for computer systems instead of people, and Zara, whose whole job is trying doors nobody else tried, found that connection had no lock on it at all. She proved it using her own legitimate login. Now Dmitri and Zara have to stand up in front of their boss, Natalie, and explain plainly: here's everything that works, and here's exactly what almost didn't, and exactly how it got fixed before anyone outside the company ever touched it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A leadership readout about a caught security finding succeeds or fails on one decision: whether the presenters treat it as proof the review process works, or try to talk around it. This lesson is built around the former. The headline deserves to come first, because it's real: x_brind_claims is a complete scoped application -- the Warranty Claim table, a correctly-written row-level ACL, a partner self-service portal, Flow Designer routing automation, and a Scripted REST API -- backed by a passing ATF suite and a clean UAT with three real partner companies.

Naming the vulnerability by its exact mechanism, not "we found a security issue," is what lets Natalie trust the fix rather than just accept an apology: the GET handler for `/api/x_brind_claims/claims` filtered strictly by whatever `partner_company` value the caller supplied, using plain GlideRecord, which does not automatically evaluate the table's ACL the way the native UI does. The ACL itself was never wrong -- it correctly protected the portal the entire time. The script simply never asked it anything. It's also worth stating plainly that UAT was never going to catch this: Holly Vance's integration test in lesson 14 queried for Driscoll's own data and got exactly that back, which is a completely different test than one partner's credentials requesting another partner's data through the same endpoint. That's deliberately a security review's job, not UAT's.

The frame that keeps this presentation honest rather than defensive is that finding this now -- during a planned pre-launch security review, before a single partner's commercially sensitive claim data was ever exposed to a direct competitor -- is the review step doing precisely the job it was scoped to do. Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners often compete directly in the same local markets, and a leaked `resolution_notes` field can describe exactly how a competitor's equipment failure was diagnosed and repaired. No partner data actually leaked outside Brindlewood's own testing, and the fix required zero changes to the ACL -- only the one script needed to start consulting it. That distinction, a caught pre-launch defect rather than a live incident, is the one Natalie most needs to hear stated precisely.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with what this presentation covers, in order

Dmitri tells the room directly: this update covers two things. First, the real Partner Warranty Claims application that's now complete and ready for go-live. Second, a real vulnerability the team's own pre-launch security review caught -- what it was, how it was found, and how it's fixed. Lead with the first part; burying a genuinely successful build under nothing but vulnerability detail reads as far more alarming than the situation actually is.

## Step 2 -- State what's built and tested, plainly, first

```
PARTNER WARRANTY CLAIMS (x_brind_claims) -- WHAT'S READY TODAY
Scoped app:   x_brind_claims_warranty_claim table (partner_company,
              equipment_serial, issue_description, state,
              labor_hours, parts_cost, resolution_notes)
Access:       Row-level ACL restricting each partner to their own
              company's claims
Portal:       Partner self-service -- submit a claim, view "My
              Warranty Claims"
Automation:   Flow Designer routes new claims to the right reviewer
API:          Scripted REST API for partner integrations
Testing:      ATF suite passing; UAT clean across Driscoll, Castle
              Rock Tooling, and Vantage Precision Group
Status:       Fixed and re-verified; ready for go-live
```

## Step 3 -- Name the vulnerability by its exact mechanism

```
ZARA:    During my pre-launch security review, I called the GET
         /api/x_brind_claims/claims endpoint directly, authenticated
         as a real Driscoll test user, but passed Castle Rock
         Tooling's partner_company value instead of Driscoll's own.
         I got Castle Rock Tooling's claim back anyway -- including
         resolution_notes. The handler used plain GlideRecord, which
         doesn't automatically enforce our table's ACL the way the
         portal does. Our ACL was never wrong -- the script just
         never asked it anything.
```

## Step 4 -- Explain why this matters commercially, not just technically

Natalie needs this stated once, directly: Brindlewood's roughly 200 partners frequently compete against each other in the same local service markets, and `resolution_notes` can describe exactly how a competitor's equipment failure was diagnosed and fixed. This was a real, exploitable, commercially damaging leak -- not a theoretical one -- and it is the exact scenario the security review existed to catch before go-live.

## Step 5 -- State the fix, specifically

```
FIX:
1. Swapped new GlideRecord() for new GlideRecordSecure() in the GET
   handler -- a drop-in change with the identical query API.
2. Re-ran Zara's exact scenario: same Driscoll credentials, same
   foreign partner_company value. Result now comes back empty.
3. Re-ran a legitimate request: Driscoll credentials, Driscoll's own
   partner_company value. Driscoll's own claim still returns
   correctly.
4. Added a permanent ATF test and a standing pre-launch security-
   checklist entry so this class of bug is caught automatically on
   any future integration.
```

## Step 6 -- Frame the finding correctly

The right frame is not "we almost shipped something broken." It's: "our planned pre-launch security review did exactly what it was scoped to do -- it found a real, exploitable cross-partner leak before any partner's commercially sensitive claim data was ever exposed to a competitor, and the fix is now permanently guarded by an automated test."

## Step 7 -- Rehearse the hard questions

```
Q: Why didn't UAT catch this?
A: UAT tested each partner's own integration pulling their own data
   -- exactly what it's designed for. It never tried one partner's
   credentials requesting another partner's data. That's a security
   review's job, not UAT's.

Q: Could the same bug exist in other integrations?
A: We've confirmed the fix on this specific API. We have not yet
   audited every other Scripted REST API at Brindlewood for the same
   pattern -- that's real, named follow-up work, not something we're
   claiming is covered here.
```

## Step 8 -- Close by asking for explicit understanding

Ask Natalie and the room to confirm two things clearly: why the original script was exploitable, and that the fix plus the new permanent ATF test are both already in place and re-verified. That confirmation, not a smooth delivery, is what this presentation is actually for.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Presented the finished x_brind_claims build to Natalie -- table, ACL, portal, Flow Designer routing, API, passing ATF suite, clean three-partner UAT -- then walked through the cross-partner leak precisely: the GET handler's plain-GlideRecord query never consulting the table's already-correct ACL, Zara's proof using Driscoll credentials against Castle Rock's partner_company value, and the fix (GlideRecordSecure swap, re-verification, permanent ATF test, standing checklist entry).
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Got Natalie and leadership aligned on the real state of the build: the partner claims system is complete, tested, and UAT-clean, and we gave a specific, honest account of the cross-partner data leak our internal security review caught -- what it was, who found it, and exactly what changed. Natalie confirmed she understands why the original API was exploitable and that the fix is already verified.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found and fixed a real vulnerability in our new partner claims system before it ever touched a real partner's sensitive data, through the security review step we planned specifically to catch this kind of thing. Given how often our partners compete directly against each other, catching this now -- internally, before go-live -- is the review process working exactly as intended, not a problem with the build.

lessons.title: From API to Real Partner Workflow, Day to Day
lessons.summary: Translating the finished, security-reviewed Partner Warranty Claims system into what Driscoll Mechanical Services' Holly Vance actually experiences day to day -- submitting a claim through the portal, Flow Designer routing it to the right reviewer, and checking status through the portal or her own API integration -- and the honest boundary: no automated parts ordering yet, and self-service built for partners only, not Brindlewood's own internal claims team.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the security finding presented and the fix verified, this lesson follows x_brind_claims the rest of the way -- out of the review room and into an actual partner's day. Holly Vance, Driscoll Mechanical Services' IT contact, logs into the live portal, submits a real warranty claim for a piece of Driscoll's equipment, watches Flow Designer route it to the right reviewer automatically, and checks its status either through the portal's "My Warranty Claims" list or by calling the now-secured Scripted REST API herself with Driscoll's own `partner_company` value.

This lesson also states, honestly and without apology, two real boundaries that remain. First, there is no automated parts-ordering or inventory integration tied to an approved claim -- once a claim is resolved, Driscoll still orders replacement parts through Brindlewood's existing, separate process, exactly as it did before this project. That gap was named and deliberately deferred back in lesson 3 as a real V2 idea, not something anyone forgot. Second, self-service in V1 was built for partners only -- Brindlewood's own internal employees who review and resolve claims still work largely through back-end list views, not a dedicated internal-facing UI. Both are real, scoped-out edges of what V1 was ever meant to cover, not oversights being hidden from Holly or from Brindlewood's own team.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you order a part for your car from a shop's website. You fill out a form describing what's broken, the website automatically sends your request to the right mechanic without you having to call anyone, and you can check on your phone whether it's done yet. That's a genuinely good system -- but it doesn't mean everything about car repair is automatic now. If the mechanic needs to order a new part, you still have to call the parts store the old-fashioned way, because nobody's connected that part yet. And the mechanics themselves, inside the shop, are still writing most repair notes on paper clipboards instead of using a fancy app of their own.

That's exactly where Brindlewood Industrial's new claims system stands. Holly, at one of Brindlewood's partner companies, can submit a warranty claim online, watch it get routed to the right person automatically, and check its status any time -- a real, working improvement. But when a claim needs replacement parts ordered, that still happens the old way. And Brindlewood's own employees, the people actually fixing the equipment, mostly still work from plain lists on their own screens, not a shiny new app built just for them. Both of those are true today, said out loud rather than glossed over.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A system only earns its place in a real product the moment it maps onto an actual user's day, not just a passing functional test. For Holly Vance, that day breaks into three concrete moments, each one directly traceable to a component built across lessons 5 through 12. Submit: she logs into the partner portal, fills in `equipment_serial` and `issue_description`, and the row-level ACL -- now confirmed enforced consistently across both the portal and, since the fix, the API -- ensures the record is stamped with Driscoll's own `partner_company` and visible only to Driscoll. Route: Flow Designer picks up the new record and assigns it to the correct reviewer or assignment group without anyone at Brindlewood manually triaging an inbox. Check status: Holly either opens "My Warranty Claims" in the portal, or, since her team built their own integration back in lesson 14's UAT, calls `GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims?partner_company=<Driscoll's own value>` directly -- now running through GlideRecordSecure, so the same request that once could have returned a competitor's data is guaranteed to return only Driscoll's own.

The honest boundary matters just as much as the workflow, because overstating V1's reach the moment it works well for one partner is exactly the kind of overclaim this series has already shown the cost of skipping scrutiny on. No automated parts-ordering or inventory integration exists yet -- a resolved claim doesn't trigger anything downstream; Driscoll still orders replacement parts through Brindlewood's existing, separate process. That's not an oversight; it was named and deliberately deferred back in lesson 3 as real, scoped V2 work, and it's worth naming here again as a concrete next step rather than a vague someday. Equally, V1's self-service was scoped to partners specifically -- Brindlewood's own internal reviewers still work the claim largely through standard back-end list views, not a dedicated internal portal UI built for their workflow. Both gaps are real, bounded, and worth saying plainly to anyone asking "is this done" -- because the honest answer is that the partner-facing core is done and working, and these two pieces are deliberately, visibly, not yet built.

lessons.title: Writing the Security Review Report and Developer Handoff
lessons.summary: The actual internal security review report for the cross-partner data leak -- severity, proof of exploit, fix, and verification -- plus developer handoff documentation covering the ACL design, the Scripted REST API's contract, and the standing security-checklist entry, with ownership named by person: Dmitri on the application and API, Zara on ongoing security review, Owen on platform-level ACL and role administration.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A vulnerability that only lives in Zara's and Dmitri's memory is a liability the moment either of them is unavailable the next time something similar needs reviewing. This lesson writes the two documents that prevent that: a real internal security review report -- the cross-partner data leak in the GET `/claims` endpoint, its severity, a reproducible proof of exploit, the fix that was applied, and confirmation that the fix was verified against that exact exploit -- stated with the precision a future auditor or new team member would need to trust it without taking anyone's word for it, plus a concrete developer handoff document: what x_brind_claims actually is, how the row-level ACL is designed, the Scripted REST API's exact contract (endpoint, required and optional parameters, response shape), and the standing security-checklist entry now required on any future integration against an ACL'd table.

This lesson also names ownership plainly, going forward: Dmitri Kowalski owns the application and its API, Zara Ahmed owns ongoing security review -- including deciding when this class of check needs to run again -- and Owen Castellano owns platform-level ACL and role administration.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a home inspector who checks a house before someone buys it. She doesn't just say "looks fine now" -- she writes down exactly what she found, how serious it was, exactly how she proved it was a real problem, and exactly what the builder changed to fix it, so the next inspector who looks at the house doesn't have to start from scratch or just take her word for it. Then, separately, someone writes a clear handbook for whoever moves in next: here's how the locks work, here's which door connects to which room, here's the rule we now follow every time we add a new door.

That's exactly what this lesson does for Brindlewood's claims system. It writes down, precisely, what the data-leak problem was, how bad it could have been, exactly how Zara proved it was real, and exactly what Dmitri changed to fix it -- so anyone who reads it later can trust it without having to take anyone's word for it. And it writes a real handbook for the next developer: what the system tracks, how the locks (the ACL) are supposed to work, exactly what the data connection (the API) promises to whoever calls it, and the new permanent rule the team now follows.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A security review report earns its place in the organization's memory only if every claim in it is specific and checkable, not a narrative impression. "We found and fixed a security issue" is not a finding; "the GET handler for `/api/x_brind_claims/claims` filtered strictly by the client-supplied `partner_company` query parameter using plain GlideRecord, which does not enforce table ACLs the way the native UI does, and never checked that parameter against the authenticated caller's own company -- severity: critical, confirmed exploitable by authenticating as a real Driscoll Mechanical Services test user and passing Castle Rock Tooling's `partner_company` value" is. The proof-of-exploit section matters most for exactly this reason: a finding is only as credible as its reproduction steps, so the report states precisely what request was sent and what response came back, not just that the exploit worked.

The fix section needs the same precision: the exact one-line change from `GlideRecord` to `GlideRecordSecure`, why that specific replacement closes the gap without touching the rest of the handler's logic, and the specific verification step -- re-running Zara's exact scenario against the fixed script and confirming it now returns nothing, while a legitimate same-company request still succeeds.

The developer handoff document needs the same specificity a new engineer would actually need to safely extend this application: the table's field list, the ACL's exact logic (compare the logged-in user's company to the record's `partner_company`), the API's full contract -- `partner_company` required, `state` and `equipment_serial` optional -- and the standing checklist rule this incident produced: any future Scripted REST API or Script Include querying an ACL'd table must be tested by directly calling it as a low-privilege user attempting to retrieve another company's data, not just confirmed to return "my own data correctly." Ownership needs the same precision: Dmitri Kowalski owns the application and API code going forward, Zara Ahmed owns ongoing security review and decides when this class of check needs to run again on future integrations, and Owen Castellano owns platform-level ACL and role administration -- the layer the API fix now correctly depends on.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the security review report header

```
INTERNAL SECURITY REVIEW REPORT -- x_brind_claims SCRIPTED REST API
Reviewer:  Zara Ahmed, ServiceNow Technical Architect, Brindlewood
           Industrial
Scope:     GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims
Method:    Direct REST client testing, authenticated as a real
           partner test user, querying outside the partner's own
           company
Status:    One critical finding, fixed and re-verified
```

## Step 2 -- Write the finding precisely

```
FINDING: Broken access control / missing ACL enforcement [CRITICAL]

The GET handler filtered strictly by whatever partner_company value
the caller supplied, using plain GlideRecord, which does not
automatically evaluate table ACLs the way the native UI does. It
never checked that value against the authenticated caller's own
company. The table's read ACL is correctly written and correctly
protects the portal -- it was simply never consulted here.

IMPACT: any authenticated partner API user could retrieve any other
partner's warranty claims, including commercially sensitive
resolution_notes, by passing a different partner_company value.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the proof of exploit, reproducibly

```
PROOF OF EXPLOIT:
GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims?partner_company=<Castle_Rock_Tooling_sys_id>
Authorization: Basic <Driscoll Mechanical Services test user credentials>

Response: Castle Rock Tooling's claim returned in full, including
resolution_notes -- despite the request being authenticated purely
as a Driscoll Mechanical Services account.
```

## Step 4 -- Write the fix and its verification

```
FIX APPLIED: replaced new GlideRecord('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim')
with new GlideRecordSecure('x_brind_claims_warranty_claim') in the GET
handler -- a drop-in replacement; no other logic changed.

VERIFICATION: re-ran the exact proof-of-exploit request above against
the fixed script. Result: empty array. Re-ran the same request with
Driscoll's own partner_company value: Driscoll's own claim returned
correctly. A permanent ATF test now covers this exact scenario.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the developer handoff document

```
DEVELOPER HANDOFF -- x_brind_claims (Partner Warranty Claims)

TABLE: x_brind_claims_warranty_claim
  Fields: partner_company, equipment_serial, issue_description,
          state, labor_hours, parts_cost, resolution_notes

ACL DESIGN: Read access restricted by comparing the logged-in user's
  company to the record's partner_company field. Correctly enforced
  in the portal and, since the fix, in the API via GlideRecordSecure.

API CONTRACT: GET /api/x_brind_claims/claims
  Required: partner_company
  Optional: state, equipment_serial
  Returns only records the authenticated caller's ACL permits.

STANDING CHECKLIST ENTRY: any future Scripted REST API or Script
  Include against an ACL'd table must be tested by calling it as a
  low-privilege user attempting another company's data -- not just
  confirmed to return "my own data correctly."
```

## Step 6 -- Name ownership plainly

```
OWNERSHIP, GOING FORWARD
  Application and API:          Dmitri Kowalski (ServiceNow Developer)
  Ongoing security review:      Zara Ahmed (ServiceNow Technical
                                 Architect)
  Platform ACL / role admin:    Owen Castellano (ServiceNow Platform
                                 Administrator)
  Business sponsor:             Natalie Fairweather (Director of
                                 Partner Operations)
```

## Step 7 -- Store it where the next reader will find it

Save both documents in Brindlewood's shared engineering repository, link the report directly from the checklist entry in the handoff document, and walk Owen and Natalie through both, since Owen executes the checklist on future integrations and Natalie will need the report's precise language the first time a partner or auditor asks what was found and fixed.
