Wrote the developer handoff covering the table's fields, the ACL's exact logic, the API's full contract, and the standing checklist entry. Ownership named: Dmitri on the app/API, Zara on ongoing security review, Owen on platform ACL/role administration.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Produced the real security documentation and developer handoff: a precise, reproducible finding and fix write-up, plus a clear reference for anyone who extends this system later. Ownership is named by person -- Dmitri owns the app and API, Zara owns ongoing security review, Owen owns platform-level access control -- so nothing falls through the cracks going forward.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've written down exactly what the security issue was, how it was proven real, and how it was fixed, in language precise enough for anyone reviewing this later to trust without taking our word for it. We also have clear ownership going forward: our developer owns the application, our architect owns ongoing security review, and our platform administrator owns access control.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Shipped, What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the Partner Warranty Claims build -- what's genuinely live and security-reviewed, and the three real gaps left for a future phase: no automated parts-ordering integration, no systematic audit of other integrations for the same ACL-bypass class of bug, and internal employees still on back-end list views. Series complete.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last lesson in the series, and like the project it closes out, it is not a highlight reel. Over nineteen prior lessons, Brindlewood Industrial went from Natalie Fairweather's business problem -- roughly 200 partner companies with no real way to self-serve warranty claims -- to a real, working x_brind_claims scoped application: a correctly-designed Warranty Claim table, a row-level ACL, a partner self-service portal, Flow Designer routing automation, and a Scripted REST API. That build went through its own planned pre-launch security review, found a genuine, critical cross-partner data leak in the API's GET handler, and fixed it -- swapping in GlideRecordSecure, re-verifying the exact exploit now fails, and permanently adding both an ATF test and a security-checklist entry -- without needing to touch the already-correct ACL at all.

What this lesson does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what is still manual, unaudited, or deliberately out of scope, so whoever reads this next isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud. Three real gaps get named plainly: no automated parts-ordering or inventory integration tied to approved claims, no systematic audit of Brindlewood's other existing ServiceNow integrations for the same class of ACL-bypass bug, and self-service built for partners only -- Brindlewood's own internal employees still work largely through back-end list views, not a dedicated internal-facing UI. None of them are failures. All three are honest, scoped-out boundaries of what this build was ever meant to cover.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months helping a company build a new website so its outside partners could finally handle their own paperwork online instead of emailing it back and forth. Partway through, your own safety inspector found a real way one partner could have accidentally seen another partner's private information -- and you fixed it yourselves before anyone outside the company ever saw it happen. That's genuinely good work. But a good team doesn't just hand over the keys and call it perfect. They say plainly: ordering replacement parts still happens the old way, nobody's gone back and checked every other similar system for the same kind of mistake, and the company's own employees are still using plain lists instead of a nice new screen built just for them.

That's this whole lesson, for Brindlewood's claims system. The partner-facing website is real, it works, and it already caught and fixed a real security problem before launch. But parts ordering isn't automatic yet, nobody's double-checked every other system for the same bug, and Brindlewood's own team still works from plain lists. Dmitri and Zara say all three things clearly instead of pretending the job is completely, permanently done.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it states the real deliverable plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen lessons could still understand exactly what's running, and it names the actual remaining gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the data-leak finding itself -- not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations with a reason. For x_brind_claims, three are worth stating without softening.

First, there is no automated parts-ordering or inventory integration tied to an approved claim. Driscoll, Castle Rock Tooling, and Vantage Precision Group all still order replacement parts through Brindlewood's existing, separate process after a claim resolves. This was named and deliberately deferred back in lesson 3 as real V2 work -- a genuine next step, not an oversight. Second, there has been no systematic audit of Brindlewood's other existing ServiceNow integrations and Scripted REST APIs for the same class of ACL-bypass bug Zara found in this one. The team fixed this specific API; nobody has yet gone back through every other existing integration asking the same question Zara asked about this one. That's a real, open risk worth naming precisely rather than assuming the fix here somehow covers everything else. Third, self-service in V1 was scoped to partners only -- Brindlewood's own internal employees who review and resolve claims still work largely through standard back-end list views, not a dedicated internal-facing UI; that's real, scoped-out follow-on work, not something this build was ever asked to cover.

Naming these three is not an admission of failure; overselling completeness right after this team already lived through finding one real vulnerability would itself repeat the exact mistake the security review already taught this room to take seriously. The honest version of done is: this build solved the specific, real problem it was scoped to solve, found and fixed one real vulnerability along the way through its own planned process, and here are its real remaining edges and what comes next.

## Step 1 -- State the finished deliverable in one pass, end to end

```
ORIGIN:          Natalie Fairweather needed Brindlewood's roughly 200
                 partner companies to self-serve warranty claims
                 instead of emailing them back and forth
APPLICATION:     x_brind_claims -- Warranty Claim table
                 (partner_company, equipment_serial,
                 issue_description, state, labor_hours, parts_cost,
                 resolution_notes)
ACCESS:          Row-level ACL restricting each partner to their own
                 company's claims
PORTAL:          Partner self-service -- submit a claim, track status
AUTOMATION:      Flow Designer routes new claims to the right
                 reviewer automatically
API:             Scripted REST API for partner integrations
TESTING:         ATF suite passing; UAT clean across Driscoll
                 Mechanical Services, Castle Rock Tooling, and
                 Vantage Precision Group
VULNERABILITY FOUND & FIXED: a critical cross-partner data leak in
                 the API's GET handler -- plain GlideRecord never
                 consulting the table's already-correct ACL. Found
                 by Zara Ahmed via direct REST testing as a real
                 Driscoll test user against a foreign
                 partner_company value. Fixed by swapping in
                 GlideRecordSecure, with a permanent ATF test and
                 security-checklist entry added -- no change needed

DOCUMENTATION:   A precise security review report with reproducible
                 proof of exploit and fix, plus developer handoff
                 documentation naming ownership by person.
STATUS:          Ready for go-live.
```

Every line above was built, tested, and is genuinely true today -- that is the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 -- Name what's still manual, unaudited, or out of scope, specifically

```
GAP 1: No automated parts-ordering or inventory integration tied to
  an approved claim. Partners still order replacement parts through
  Brindlewood's existing, separate process. Named and deliberately
  deferred back in lesson 3 as real V2 work.

GAP 2: No systematic audit of Brindlewood's OTHER existing
  ServiceNow integrations and Scripted REST APIs for the same
  ACL-bypass class of bug. This API was fixed specifically; nobody
  has gone back through every other existing integration asking the
  same question Zara asked about this one.

GAP 3: No dedicated internal-facing UI. Brindlewood's own internal
  employees who review and resolve claims still work largely through
  back-end list views, not a purpose-built interface. V1 scoped
  self-service for partners specifically.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
This project took Brindlewood Industrial's partner warranty claims
process from manual email back-and-forth to a complete, tested,
security-reviewed scoped application -- a correctly-designed table,
row-level ACL, partner self-service portal, Flow Designer routing,
and a Scripted REST API, ready for go-live. It found and fixed a
real, critical cross-partner data leak during its own planned
pre-launch security review, through Zara Ahmed's direct testing and
a working proof of exploit, and it left behind documentation precise
enough for a future reviewer to trust without taking anyone's word
for it. It did not build automated parts ordering, a systematic audit
of other integrations for the same bug class, or an internal-facing
UI for Brindlewood's own team -- those are real, named gaps, not
oversights pretending not to exist.
```

## Step 4 -- Leave a short, prioritized list for a future phase

```
1. Audit Brindlewood's other existing ServiceNow integrations and
   Scripted REST APIs for the same plain-GlideRecord-against-an-
   ACL'd-table pattern. Closes Gap 2 -- the highest-value item, since
   this incident already proved the pattern exists at least once and
   an unaudited integration elsewhere carries the identical risk.
2. Scope and build an automated parts-ordering or inventory
   integration tied to approved claims. Closes Gap 1.
3. Scope a dedicated internal-facing UI for Brindlewood's own claims
   reviewers, distinct from the partner portal. Closes Gap 3.
```

## Step 5 -- Close the series the way it should close: honestly, not triumphantly

This is the last lesson of twenty. Resist the pull to end on an unqualified victory lap. The real ending is: Brindlewood built a working partner self-service application that caught and fixed a real, critical vulnerability through its own planned security process -- which is a better outcome than an application that never finds out its blind spots exist until a partner does. Three honest, specific limitations remain, named and handed off instead of hidden. That's a finished build, not a perfect one -- and that's the whole point of telling it this way.

Series complete.

Named three real gaps rather than glossing over them: no automated parts-ordering integration, no systematic audit of other integrations for the same ACL-bypass bug class, and no dedicated internal-facing UI for Brindlewood's own reviewers.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Wrapped the project with an honest accounting of what shipped versus what's still open. The application, automation, testing, and the fixed vulnerability are genuinely done -- that part is real. We also have a short, prioritized list for a future phase, led by auditing our other integrations for the same bug pattern, so nothing gets rediscovered as a surprise later.

We're also telling you plainly what this doesn't cover yet -- parts ordering isn't automated, we haven't checked our other systems for the same type of bug, and our own internal team still works from plain lists rather than a dedicated screen.
